HARRY L. MAYNARD

HARRY L. MAYNARD
Grand Master
October 13, 1982-0ctober 12, 1983

The expression, "If you want a job done give it to a busy man," was
never better illustrated than in the case of Harry Lee Maynard, the 117th
Grand Master of Masons in California and Hawaii. His boundless energy
and enthusiasm for the task of leading the Masonic Fraternity in these two
States were amply demonstrated on a daily basis throughout the 1982-1983
Grand Lodge year. His attention to the many details of planning which
are inherent in the office of Grand Master was reflected time and again in
the administrative and ceremonial functions of the Grand Lodge of California.
As Grand Master he was extremely proud of the fact that he was privileged to have had the opportunity to officiate at the chartering of four
new Masonic Lodges, something not accorded to any Grand Master since
1964. Early in his term of office, Brother Maynard arranged for a Grand
Master's tour of the South Pacific, inviting the Brethren of our Jurisdiction
and their families to take advantage of the opportunity to visit Australia
and New Zealand. He personally led the first group of some two hundred
on a marvelous two week journey to these countries where they were
received and entertained by two Australian Grand Lodges and one of the
Constituent Lodges in New Zealand. A firm bond of Masonic friendship
was thus established between the Brethren and ladies "down under" and
those who partook of this exciting journey - a bond which hopefully will
long endure between our respective jurisdictions.
Born on November 5, 1927 in DeWitt, Iowa, our future Grand Master
attended both elementary and high school in that community, graduating
from high school in 1945. His college education began at Colgate University in 1945-1946 due to his service in the United States Navy as an aviation
cadet in the Navy }1-5 program, after which he attended several institutions
of higher learning and in 1950 received a Bachelor of Arts degree in physical education, mathematics and physics at the University of Northern
Iowa.
It was while our future Grand Master was teaching school and. coaching
in Stuart, Iowa, that a friendship was developed with one of his students,
Carolyn Messersmith, which eventually blossomed into true love and on
June 22, 1952, he and Carolyn were married. They became the proud
parents of a son, Harry Lee, Jr., who they lost due to an accidental death
at age five and a half, and of a daughter, Linda, who subsequently served
as Honored Queen of Bethel No. 89, International Order of Job's Daughters, and encouraged her father during his Masonic career.
Harry and Carolyn moved to Ventura, California in July 1952 and since
1959 he has been engaged in the banking profession, currently serving as
President, Chief Executive Officer and Director of the American Commercial Bank located in Ventura.
Active in numerous civic, service, professional and fraternal organizations, one wonders how this busy man found the time to attend to the
multitudinous duties incumbent upon the office of Grand Master, but find
the time he did, never neglecting his family or his professional responsibilities.
iii

His devotion to Blue Lodge Masonry is evidenced by his more than
twenty years of service to the Craft. He became a Mason in 1960 on the
recommendation of his uncle, Brother Max Randolph, oeing raised on
October 25th of that year in San Buenaventura Lodge No. 214. Progressing
through the subordinate stations of the Lodge he was elected Master and
served as such during the year 1968. His vital interests in Masonry and
Masonic affairs soon identified him as a proper individual to serve on
various Committees and Boards of the Grand Lodge. Recognizing his
unique abilities, he was selected as the nominee for the office of Junior
Grand Warden, and in October of 1979 he was elected and installed in
this important station. In 1980 he was elected Senior Grand Warden, in
1981 Deputy Grand Master and in October of 1982 he was accorded the
honor of being elected and installed to the highest station that Masonry
affords, that of Grand Master.
Brother Maynard has been and continues to be very active in the Santa
Barbara Valley with plural membership in Ventura County Valley of the
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, and by election of
the Supreme Council of the Thirty-third Degree in 1979 he was coroneted
a 33rd degree Mason. To round out his Masonic career, our Grand Master
is also a member of the York Rite and the Shrine as well as several of the
other concordant and appendant bodies of Masonry.
His ready wit and sense of humor were always displayed as he and
Carolyn traveled extensively throughout the Jurisdiction, charming all who
were privileged to come into contact with this most engaging couple. Their
friendly, gracious and sincere manner struck a responsive chord in the
hearts of the Brethren and their families, and thus it can be truly said that
as the Grand Master and as the first lady of Masonry in California and
Hawaii, Harry and Carolyn Maynard portray the true Masonic couple,
exemplifying Masonry at its best. Our Grand Master will long be remembered for his complete and total dedication to the principles, tenets and
teachings of our Masonic Fraternity and to the leadership he provided in
his quiet, efficient and business-like manner. To Grand Master Maynard
the Masons of this Jurisdiction say thank you for your devoted service in
the past and for your continuing efforts in the future.

ONE HUNDRED THIRTY-FOURTH
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California commenced its One Hundred Thirty-fourth Annual
Communication in the California Masonic Memorial Temple, San Francisco, California on Monday October 10, 1983, A.L. 5983, at 9:00 A.M.
Prior to Grand Lodge opening, Grand Organist James C. Myers entertained the assembled Brethren with an organ concert, playing the following
selections: Windor's "Toccata," W. A. Mozart's "Fantasia & Sonata," Ferde
Grofe's "Mardi Gras," "Serenata" by LeRoy Anderson, "South of the
Border" by Carr and "The Stars and Stripes Forever" by Sousa. Grand
Lodge was raised by Jesse A. Atkinson, Master of San Buenaventura
Lodge No. 214 and C. Mark Franek, Master of Poinsettia Lodge No. 633.
The gavel used opening the Morning Session was the gavel and sounding
block presented to the Grand Master by his daughter Linda and wife
Carolyn at his Installation on October 13, 1982. Other gavels used during
the Morning Session were as follow: gavel and sounding block in case
presented by the 512th Masonic District at the Opening of Grand Lodge
in Camarillo and used during the relaying of the Cornerstone of the Ventura County Masonic Memorial Center; gavel on a stand presented at
opening of Grand Lodge in Camarillo and used to strike the cornerstone
on "Well Formed, True & Trusty" on relaying for that building; mounted
gavel presented at Reception for Grand Master in Camarillo by 510th
Masonic District; gavel presented at Cornerstone Ceremony at Camarillo
by 512th Masonic District and used at Las Colinas Elementary School;
gavel and sounding block presented at Cornerstone Ceremony for the
Lemonwood Elementary School in Oxnard; gavel and sounding block
presented at relaying of Cornerstone for Franklin Elementary School in
Santa Barbara by 508th Masonic District; gavel presented at Annual Barbeque of Poinsettia Lodge No.633 in Camp Comfort; square-shaped gavel
presented at Reception by Ventura Scottish Rite Bodies in Camarillo.
Upon the call of the roll, the following Elected and Appointed Officers

Invocation
Our God and God of our Fathers: We humbly invoke Thy blessing upon
those gathered within these precincts who have assembled to further the
cause of this great, ancient and honored Fraternity. We pray that Thou
wilt continue to shower Thy grace upon the brethren through the radiance
of Thy Great Light, the luminous word of Holy Writ. Grant, 0 Heavenly
Father, that we may all stand erect on the level of integrity and brotherhood with one another; and that we may constantly remain on the square
with Thee in truth, justice and mercy. May the call of a distressed brother
never be muffled to our ears, nor the cause of righteousness alien to our
hearts. Amen.

Devotional
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
I remember, many years ago, shortly after being raised, how intrigued I
was by hearing Masons say on several occasions, "I don't need religion;
Masonry is my religion." My instinctive reaction was to reply, "How wrong
can you be!"
These brethren probably meant well, but their thinking was sadly inaccurate. For Masonry, though religious in spirit, is not religion, and cannot take the place of religion. It is true that Masonry believes in a Supreme
Deity and in immortality of the soul and has its own ceremonies which it

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7

cherishes and reveres. But these points of resemblance to religion are far
outweighed by points of difference. Masonry does not profess revelation;
it has no sacred literature such as the Old Testament, the New Testament,
or the Koran; it postulates no dogmas, carries out no sacraments, possesses
no clergy or seminaries.
Its rituals are not life-pervasive. It has no dietary laws, such as the Jews
and Catholics have, regulating the food you eat; it has no liturgy or prayers .
such as the Lord's Prayer of Protestantis m, the Ave Maria of Catholicism,
and Alenu Leshabeah of Judaism, with their respective attendant rituals;
nor has it anything similar to the great hymologies of these three faiths,
embodying grand old hymns such as "Lead, Kindly Light" of the Protestants, the Gregorian chants of the Catholic Church, the Adon Olam of
Judaism; nor has it the weekly day of rest, or the elaborate calendar of
holy days, of the three great faiths.
.
Unlike religion, Masonry does not embrace everyone; 1f you are und~r
twenty-one, or a woman , you cannot be a Mason. You are included m
your religious fellowship by the simple act of being born - but you are not
born a Mason. In sum, Masonry does not possess the overwhelming panoply of belief and ceremony and ritual and song and prayer that exerci~es
so powerful and permanent an emotional influence on the life of the mdividual from the days of his or her birth to the drawing of the final breath.
But if Masonry does not possess all these aspects of religion, it does
have two things - and most vital they are - that religion does not ~njoy.
First, Masonry is not exclusive. A Jew, for example, cannot be a Chnst1an,
or a Christian a Jew, without forsaking his religious origin and background .
But in Masonry, anyone can belong, if he believes in God and ~ the
Immortality of "1e Soul, and earns the approval of his fellows. Consider,
for example, the usual communion breakfast. Earlier, our Christian Brethren gather in a church, our Jewish brethren in synagogue; later, af.ter
separate worship, we are all gathered together about a common breakmg
of bread, as Masons, and as brothers. This simple fact gives concrete,
emphasized focus to the phrase we have so often heard, and perhaps not
fully comprehend ed: "The Brotherhood of Man under the Fatherhood of
God."
And by way of corollary, in addition to not being exclusive, Masonry is
not divisive. The word "religion" comes from the Latin word "religio"
which means "to bind together." In spite of this, however, history has
shown far too many instances of religion.acting as a divisive force - too
many instances of discrimination against men, of persecution, of ultimate
blasphemy, of bloodshed, because of religion. Masonry, by contrast, n?t
only does not bar men of various religions, it brings them together - m
their Lodges, at brotherhood breakfasts, in the activities of Grand Lodge
by which men of all faiths are helped in their hours of distress, of physical
affliction, of weakness and loneliness in old age.
Though synagogue and church may continue to divide us, the spirit of
our brotherhood unites us, and though our prayer books may be many,
our prayer as Masons is one.
.
. .
And note: It is precisely because of this - the voluntary assoc1at1on
together of men on a basis of idealism, wherein they offer their fealty to

no man or group of men, but to all men and to Almighty God - that

together under the banner of benevolence and morality never will be
~laves. A~d conversely, this is why Masonry is so respected and encouraged

~nd t~at is why, in our own beloved country, so many of our Presidents,

. Masonry is not religion, and cannot take the place of religion. But in
its ackn~wledgment of a Supreme Being and the worth of human brothe~hood, 1t has religious basis, it has a common meeting ground with religion.
It is now over 40 years since I was raised to the sublime degree of Master
Mason. As I survey these many years and think of the countless brethren
I ha~e met ~ho have come through our portals, I am grateful for the

wh~t ~asonry has meant to them. It has warmed their hearts, stimulated

Necrology
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Guests and my Brethren
all. How does a fraternal organization such as the Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii comprised of 188,537 members say "Good-bye" to 488
deceased Brethren, if the roll were called? What vehicle do you press into
duty to convey what we feel in this moment? What communication procedure do we institute that covers the lives of our dead Brothers? By what
strange alchemy can we mix a few words in the simmering cauldron of our
feelings and create a magic potion that will adequately express what each
of you is thinking?
Manifestly, many of you here today have known these Brothers personally. You have labored together in your Lodges in our common cause.
And, I dare say, if a line were to be formed here now to give opportunity
for you to say a word about your particular Brother ... who is now absent
from your Lodge meeting ... that line would extend around this entire
edifice . . . and time would have to stand still while each recalled for us
those special things that stand out in your mind about them. It becomes
therefore, at once a monumental task and celestial joy for me to represent
each of you, as we recall those of our Craft who walk no longer among
us.

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMM ITTEE TO STUDY
THE FEf\.SIBILITY OF THE FORMATION OF A
DISTRICT GRAND LODGE OF HAWAII
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Committee Charge
.To study the feasibility of forming a District Grand Lodge of Hawaii
subordinate to and under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California, and that this committee report its findings and recommendations to
the Grand Lodge at its next AnnualCommunication.
In his message to the Grand Lodge, Grand Master Robert 0. West noted
that a District Grand Lodge "is in effect a subordinate intermediate jurisdiction between Constituent Lodges and the Grand Lodge. It gives the
opportunity for a degree of autonomy by the local grouping of Lodges,
without severing itself from the Mother Grand Lodge. If you will, it permits the child to learn to crawl before it walks or runs."
He further stated, "Your Grand Master is of the opinion that a Grand
Lodge of Hawaii is an eventuality. We believe that it is important to give
the Lodges within Hawaii the opportunity to rule themselves in some
limited manner, and at the same time to learn to govern themselves in a

20

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

structure compatible with their own requirements, which in some cases
may differ substantially from those on the Mainland."
Based upon these comments the Special Committee is of the opinion
that the charge goes beyond the determination of whether or not a District
Grand Lodge is feasible. If, in fact, the committee determines that a District Grand Lodge of Hawaii is not feasible, it would not be beyond its
purview to recommend some other means of accomplishing the stated
purposes.

The following meetings were held with the Brethren in the Hawaiian
Islands:

What Is A District Grand Lodge?
In attempting to understand what constitutes a District Grand Lodge,
the committee looked af thos~ formed by the Grand Lodges of England,
Scotland, Ireland and France. It is important, first of all, to distinguish
between the Provincial and the District Grand Lodge.
A Provincial Grand Lodge is a subordinate intermediate jurisdiction
between individual Lodges and the Grand Lodge, within national boundaries. Every county in England, Scotland and Ireland and every administrative region in France is Masonically administered by a Provincial Grand
Lodge. The Provincial Grand Lodge operates with appointed and elected
Grand Officers within its regional limits and with limited powers. Except
for the additional officers the Provincial Grand Lodge is similar to our
Masonic District pattern administered by the Inspector in California or by
the District Deputy Grand Master in other parts of the United States.
The District Grand Lodge is a subordinate intermediate jurisdiction
between the Mother Grand Lodge and the individual Lodges overseas or
in foreign lands. The District Grand Lodges were established to provide
administrative services and perform ceremonies which, because of great
distances and slow lines of communication, could not be efficiently performed by the Grand Lodge.
While District Grand Lodges may vary as to form and function between
the different Grand Lodge jurisdictions, they all derive their powers from,
and remain subordinate to the Mother Grand Lodge. They were never
intended to be a stepping stone to full Grand Lodge status.
None of the above is intended to imply that the Grand Lodge of California is in any way limited in the formation of a District Grand Lodge of
Hawaii by what now exists in other jurisdictions, or that such a body could
not be the first step toward Grand Lodge status.
Committee Procedures
The committee held two meetings to discuss how best to meet the charge
given by the Grand Lodge. It was concluded that it would be important
to meet with members of the Hawaiian Lodges to get their input and ideas
regarding the proposed District Grand Lodge. It was also decided that the
committee should not present a definitive proposal regarding the establishment of a District Grand Lodge and that no decisions would be made
until we had heard from all who had an interest in this matter.

21

May 21 - Met with Lodge members in Makiki Temple, Honolulu, at 10:00 A.M. and 3:00 P. M. The selection of
Lodges at each meeting was made by the chairman
of the committee and the District Inspectors.
May 22 - Met with members of Kilauea Lodge, Hilo at 10:00
A. M. and members.o f Kona Lodge at 7:30 P. M.
May 23 - Met with members of Lodge Maui at 7:30 P. M.
May 24 - Met with members of Kauai Lodge at 7:30 P. M.
Each of the meetings was opened with a reading of Grand Master West's
message regarding the District Grand Lodge of Hawaii and the char~e
given the Special Committee. An explanation was made. ab~mt how a District Grand Lodge is organized, its functions and how 1t differs from t~e
Provincial Grand Lodge. A general discussion then ensued about the I?1strict Grand Lodge concept but inevitably the topic turned to the subject
of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
Committee Findings
Total attendance at all of the committee meetings was 152. Opinions
varied but certain ideas and opinions were repeated often enough to warrant serious consideration by the committee. They are listed below.
•Most are of the opinion that Hawaii should have its own Grand Lodge.
The differences are as to how soon and under what circumstances.
•Those who support the Grand Lodge now, offer the following reasons:
Hawaiian Lodges can financially support a Grand Lodge. Further delay
means higher costs.
.
.
Hawaii's needs, in many instances, are different from those of the Mamland.
Hawaii is the only State which does not have its own Grand Lod~~·
Under the present arrangement it appears that no one from Hawan can
ever become Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California.
•Those who support a Grand Lodge at some future date offer the following reasons:
We cannot afford it at the present time.
Concern was expressed about the effect on their investment and future
participation in the Masonic Homes of California.
They worry about the possible loss of members, particularly those not
living in the Hawaiian Islands.
.
They need more time to strengthen the local Lodges before undertakmg
such a major step.
•The District Grand Lodge concept was not received with much enthusiasm. Those who espouse the Grand Lodge now, feel the money and
effort should support that concept. Those who propose the Grand Lodge
at a future time are concerned about the costs of a District Grand Lodge.
Both groups look upon it as another layer of government which could

22

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

conceivably delay or take the place of a regular Grand Lodge and they
ask, "what is the need?"
•Most would like to see Hawaiian Masonry move more into the mainstream of California Masonry.
•If, as has often been stated, the Grand Lodge of Hawaii will and should
become a reality, then the Grand Lodge of California should establish
guidelines as to the process and the procedures to be followed. If a vote
of the members of the Hawaiian Lodges is to be a part of this process, it
should be clearly underst ood, in advance of the vote, how the ballots are
to be counted and interpre ted.
•There is some sentiment that Hawaii is fortunate to be a part of the
Grand Lodge of California and does not need its own Grand Lodge.
•It was expressed by many that if the Special Committee determines that
a District Grand Lodge is not feasible it is important to recommend some
other course of action which would lead to the ultimate establishment of
a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
Committee Conclusions
It is clear that mixed and diverse judgments and opinions exist among
the Hawaiian Brethre n as to whether they want a Grand Lodge of Hawaii
- a sovereign Grand Lodge. It seems generally, if almost totally agreed,
that a Grand Lodge is to be found someday in Hawaii. Some say, "we are
ready and we can do it," while others say, "we must know exactly what
our responsibilities, especially financial, would be." Although our committee was charged to study the feasibility of a District Grand Lodge for
and in Hawaii, all discussions we have had in our informal meetings have
tended to revolve around the question of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
The propone nts of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii seem to have one or both
of two motives. One is the natural result of Hawaii's statehood and the
desire to be a separate and equal entity in Freemasonry as well as in
statehood. The other motive is in the expressed desire to establish Hawaii's
own rules and regulations designed to fit what the proponents state are
the special and peculiar needs of Hawaii as distinguished from California.
The oppone nts are conservatively concerned about the cost of proper
operation of a small Grand Lodge, and they would have some question as
to the standing of their Grand Lodge in the Masonic World. There is also
some apprehension about the possible influence which some members of
prerequisite Masonic groups might have on the Hawaiian Grand Lodge.
Some have expressed rather pointedly their pride in being a part of one
of the world's most prestigious Grand Lodges.
One thing upon which there seems to be almost unanimous agreement
is that there needs to be a clearly defined course of action which might
lead to the ultimate formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii. The various
attempts which have been made to start a Grand Lodge and the several
elections which have been held on the subject have created considerable
strain among members of the Masonic Lodges. The Hawaiian Masons are
as dedicated and sincere as any in the world and all they ask is clear
direction in this vitally important matter.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

23

A District Grand Lodge, as the term appears to be used throughout the
Masonic World, does not seem applicable to Hawaii. Although Grand
Master West suggested it as an intermediate step toward establishment of
a Grand Lodge of Hawaii, it is difficult to see just how such an entity
would really provide anything of value to the Hawaiian Lodges. So- called
self-governance subject to the approval of the Grand Lodge of California
seems but a meaningless favor extended to Lodges already well-governed
under the rules and regulations of the Grand Lodge of California. In
addition, the costs involved in establishing a District Grand Lodge would
probably have to be borne by the Lodges in Hawaii and this might impose
quite a heavy burden.
Finally, the lack of enthusiasm on the part of the Masons in Hawaii for
a District Grand Lodge would seem to argue against attempting such a
step.
Considering all of the above it appears to this committee that establishing a District Grand Lodge of Hawaii is neither feasible nor desirable.
In looking at other alternatives the committee discussed the possibility
of creating another Division in Hawaii composed ·of three Inspectoral Districts and an Assistant Grand Lecturer. This would serve to give the Hawaiian Lodges definite geographical identity and it could be the first step
toward the formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii. It would help to
strengthen the ritual and also provide a vehicle by which the Grand Master
could delegate the authority to conduct appropriate Grand Lodge ceremonies in Hawaii. The costs of creating this Division would be substantially less than a District Grand Lodge and could be borne by the Grand
Lodge of California with little impact on the Constituent Lodges.
The Special <;ommittee therefore makes the following recommendations:

Commi ttee Recommendations

1. That the Grand Lodge of California establish a Division in Hawaii
consisting of an Assistant Grand Lecture r and an appropriate number
of Inspectoral Districts. The Grand Master should be empowered to
permit this Division to perform certain ceremonies, e.g. cornerstone
ceremonies, in the name of the Masons of Hawaii. (We do not expect
this to add appreciably to the budget of the Grand Lodge.)
2. That the edict by Grand Master Herbert Huebner, Octobe r 6, 1971,
prohibiting any activity on the part of the Masons in Hawaii in the
formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii, if still in force, be termina ted
and that a committee of fifteen qualified representative members of
Hawaiian Lodges should be appointed to develop plans and procedures for consideration of the formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
3. That the proposal to form a Grand Lodge of Hawaii should be submitted to a vote of the membership of the Hawaiian Lodges at an
appropr iate time after the committee has completed its tasks. The
method of voting and the interpretation of those votes must be de-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

termined in advance and be clearly understood by all participants.
In the event the proposal to form a Grand Lodge of Hawaii is rejected, the matter should not be reintroduced for a minimum period
of four years.
The following guidelines are suggested for implementation of recommendations 2 and 3:
The committee might be divided into sub-committees to study and
recommend how th~ Grand Lodge should be organized, the number
of officers required, how it will be financed, etc. A comprehensive
and realistic budget should be prepared which will tell the Masons
in Hawaii what the burden will be on the individual Lodges and
members. The committee should establish conditions which would
have to be met before any action could be taken to move toward the
establishment of a Grand Lodge. Members of the committee would
be selected by the Grand Master with the approval of the Executive
Committee. Committee activities should also be financed by the
Grand Lodge of California.
The committee wishes to express its appreciation for the opportunity to
serve the Masons of California and Hawaii in this important matter. We
also want to thank all who have taken time to meet and counsel with us.
We are particularly grateful for the courteous treatment we received from
those members in Hawaii who gave us the benefit of their input and ideas.
It is our sincere hope that we have contributed to the final solution of this
difficult and sometimes vexing problem.

GRAND MASTE R'S MESSAGE
My Brethren:
One hundred years ago at the 34th Annual Communication of this
Grand Lodge the Grand Orator, Worshipful Henry E. Highton, in his
Grand Oration quoting the Greek statesman Pericles, said, "I never ascend
the platform of the Pnyx without secretly imploring the Gods to suffer my
lips to utter no heedless words, and never allow me to forget that I am .
speaking to Athenians."
Now, one hundred years later at this, the 134th Annual Communication,
those words still apply as I address my Brethren of this Grand Lodge.
Having had the great honor of serving the Grand Lodge of California as
Grand Master, I feel the words of our departed Brother Rudyard Kipling
explain my feelings of this great Masonic experience, as he wrote in his
poem entitled "If."
If you can dream - and not make dreams your master
If you can think - and not make thoughts your aim
If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster - and
treat those two impostors just the same
If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue
Or walk with Kings nor lose the common touch
If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you
If all men count with you, but none too much
If you can fill the unforgiving minute with sixty
seconds worth of distance run
Yours is the earth and everything that's in it.

Those few lines from Kipling express the humility and fraternal love
with which I have tried to serve this Grand Lodge. Many Brethren I have
met tltis year could well be serving in this high office much better than I,
and I hope that opportunity comes to all who desire it, but as you all
know, only one can serve each year. A line spoken by an old Himalayan
priest in the movie, "The High Road to China," which we viewed on our
return from Hawaii, philosophically explains it. He said, "The oxen are
slow but the Earth is patient." Such it is that so many are qualified but
the time is short.
I have held high the Torch of Freemasonry to the best of my ability and
only Father Time will tell how far the light of that torch glowed brightly,
but now is the hour to pass that torch onward to another, hopefully burning
at least as brightly as it was when presented to me by Most Worshipful
Bob West one year ago. It is now the appropriate time to report to you
the opinion and actions of this Grand Master regarding this great Grand
Lodge for the past 12 months.

28

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GENERAL CoNDITIONS

Last year at my installation I gave you some recollections and predictions as seen in the crystal ball of Freemasonr y in this Jurisdiction.
After traveling from Crescent City in the northwest corner of our State
of California to Imperial on our southern border, and the wonderful tour
of the Lodges of our Brethren in the beautiful State of Hawaii, and the
little mountain ranching community of Stonyford and many other places
like these, I can assure you that Freemasonr y is alive and well in California
and Hawaii. Many activities are going on in the Lodges throughout the
Jurisdiction. Even the loss of membership was less this past year than for
many years, which I hope indicates that the trend is reversing in the problem of membership . In areas where there have been publicity of Grand
Lodge activities and Lodge participation in the community, it has been
shown that Masonry is coming out of the darkness of the cloak of assumed
secrecy to display the brilliant glow of its wonderful armor of shining
principles and beliefs. I remind all of you to recall the admonition that
has been given you that the burdens and responsibilities of Freemasonr y
are yours as well as your right to enjoy its benefits and its privileges. I still
believe that as the light of Freemasonr y is desired in greater intensity in
all parts of this Jurisdiction, the Annual Communica tion will be held in
other great cities in California. I urge you to consider that this gathering
of Masons would be much more recognized in other geographical areas.
Our Fraternity should not merely be taken for granted.
PROGRAMS OF GRAND LoooE

As I have traveled among our 618 Lodges I have been greatly impressed
with those Grand Lodge programs utilized by many of these Lodges. I
particularly commend our Public Schools Committee under the Chairmanship of Worshipful Bob McDonald and the Lodges and Brethren of
California not only for their own Public Schools program, but the timely
aid and support given to our State Superintend ent of Public Instruction,
Bill Honig, and other State and local officials in the passage of significant
public education legislation. Our Fraternity was very vocally and visibly
recognized by Mr. Honig and others for those efforts. I am proud of all
of you, and I know that the Torch of Freedom- Public Education- burns
more brightly because of you. Especially helpful and active in the election
of Mr. Honig and the support of this program was our Past Grand Master,
Dr. Eugene Hopp, and I personally commend him.
Our Layman's Night Speakers' Panel has been more active than ever
because you Masters of the Constituent Lodges have seen the results of
the program as applications have been forthcoming and have requested
this fine program under the coordination of its dynamic Chairman, Worshipful Irving Berliner. I urge all of you to enlist the aid of this talented
Committee in the future.
Our Wardens' Workshop Committee has also expanded its efforts and
has played a great role in leadership developmen t in our Jurisdiction, and

I know its efforts will pay dividends and its duties be even further expanded

This year I challenged each of the Masons of California and Hawaii to
show me the $1.5 million in contribution s to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund in support of our Masonic Homes. We missed by $10,740.
Thanks to the great efforts of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board
under the enthusiastic leadership of Worshipful Bob Hilts, new goals now
need to be established because of this year's outstanding effort.
The efforts of the Endowment Board are appreciated· by the Board of
Trustees of our Masonic Homes. The Board's report which will be presented by the President, Past Grand Master Kermit A. Jacobson, will give
the details, but I want to express the great thrill I received in serving on
the Board for three years as an Elective Progressive Grand Lodge Officer.
We should all be proud of this part of our heritage and support. I challenge
all Lodges to reach for 100% support of this great charity, for "our faith
may be lost in sight, hope ends in fruition, but charity extends beyond the
grave through the boundless realms of eternity."
The Standing Committee on U. S. Constitution Observance under its
new Chairman Worshipful Sherm Wicker has obtained fine support from
the Lodges, and one of our Resolutions this year addresses itself to the
fonnal duties of this Committee which will help it fulfill its rightful task
as an important committee of this Grand Lodge.
In an effort to increase the efficiency of some committees of Grand
Lodge, I have reduced the number of members on some of them and
adjusted their goals. This was done in discussion with and suggestions from
your Executive Committee, and it has been successful in some areas and
static in others. I know this attitude will continue in the future because of
common ideals of the Executive Committee. No new programs were introduced and some which I felt redundant and expensive were dropped.
Overall, we have attempted to use our programs to create Masonic awareness throughout the Jurisdiction through the fine help of all of our Inspectors, Committeem en, Grand Lodge Officers, and especially the Constituent Lodges. Keep up the good work.
An important program of the individual Lodges and recognized by this
Grand Lodge needs special mention. I feel, as some Past Grand Masters
have noted before, that the fine Hiram Award Program has been either
misundersto od or abused. This prestigious award has been given to some
who have already been adequately recognized for their service to Freemasonry. It was the original intent for a Lodge to recognize one Brother
each year who has not been Master of his Lodge, an Inspector, a Grand
Lodge Officer and, yes, even a Past Grand Master. Truly, these Brethren
all deserve recognition, but it is my belief, and others concur, that they
have been amply rewarded, and the Hiram Award should be reserved for
those who have not been so recognized by having been elected by their
peers blJ:~ who labor diligently with no hope of tangible Masonic reward.
I hope ybu will appreciate the sincerity of this observation and heed the
real intent of the Hiram Award.

GENERAL ACTIVITIES

As your Grand Master, I have attempted to fulfill my promise of last
October to take the Grand Lodge out to the Constituent Lodges and to
the individual members of this great Jurisdiction. We have opened Grand
Lodge many times for various reasons. We have layed a number of cornerstones for public buildings, public schools and especially thrilling, for
new Masonic Temples. Equally inspiring was the Burning of the Mortgage
of some Masonic Temples. This Grand Master like others before him also
dedicated Masonic Lodge Rooms, assisted in conferral of degrees when
invited, presented three 75-year pins and some 50-year Golden Veteran
Award buttons. All of these were memorable experiences but most rewarding was the Constitution of four new Lodges: Orange County Daylight Lodge No. 833, Square and Compass Lodge No. 834, Half Moon Bay .
Lodge No. 835 and Kona Lodge No. 836. The Brethren of these new
Lodges working under dispensation performed all their duties and were
granted charters at our last Annual Communication. They are now going
forward and will make a fine contribution to our Jurisdiction and to Freemasonry in general. I commend them all!
I traveled with the Deputy Grand Master and Grand Secretary to Dallas,
Texas in February to represent you at the Grand Masters' Conference of
North America. Many of the same problems we encounter in our Juris• diction were mentioned by others, and it has been said before that perhaps
the main benefit of this annual conference is in becoming acquainted with
the leaders of other jurisdictions and the mutual exchange of ideas. It was
especially rewarding to receive the accolades from many about our fine
programs and the recognition of being one of the outstanding Masonic
jurisdictions of the world. Many want to hear what California is doing. It
was my great honor to be invited to sit at the head table at the traditional
elegant luncheon hosted by Most Worshipful Henry C. Clausen, Past
Grand Master, Active 33rd degree and Sovereign Grand Commander of
the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction of the
United States at the Dallas, Texas Scottish Rite Temple.
The Grand Master's Tour of the South Pacific took place in April and
May, and we were joined by 806 travelers - Brothers and their ladies and
friends - on our journey to Melbourne in Victoria, Australia, to Sydney
in New South Wales, Australia and to Auckland, New Zealand. It was
truly a thrilling Masonic experience for we were hosted by the Grand
Lodge of each of these Jurisdictions at official Masonic meetings, informal
receptions, luncheons and barbeques. I won't take the time or chance
boring you with all the wonderful details, but I do need to tell you about
one event.
Arrangements had been made by Worshipful Tony Wordlow of Tehama
Lodge No. 3 in Sacramento, for some of us to attend the Installation of
Ruawai Lodge in a little farming community, 120 kilometers northwest of
Auckland, New Zealand. Grand Secretary Bob Klinger, Past Grand Master Lester McElwain, Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division III "Use" Pa-

tropulos, Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division IV Bill Taylor, Grand Marshal Jack W. Joe, Grand Pursuivant Davis Leonard and Worshipful Joel
Springer drove in a rented van from the wrong side of that van, on the
wrong side of the road, to this small village, arriving in time to be hosted
at a wonderful lamb barbeque at one of the member's ranch home. We
then departed to various members' homes to change into our formal wear
after which we met again at the tiny !-odge Hall for the Installation. The

opened their home and provided transportation to Brother Bennett for

the Installation, their Grand Orator offered a toast to Kevin Bennett who
was in attendanc~ though very ill. The toast was written by his friend and
Brother Tony Wordlow, and I believe it told the whole story of. the meaning
of Brotherly Love even though the two resided on opposite sides of the
earth. It was a very emotional, fraternal experience.
On June 30, we received word of the death of Worshipful Brother Kevin
Bennett of Ruawai Lodge, and he is now "happy in his Father's house."

Number ].-Creation of a Hawaiian Division
As a result of the recommendation of the Special Committee on the
Hawaiian Grand Lodge study, appointed by me on the Recommendation
of Past Grand Master Robert 0. West and adopted at the last Annual
O>mmunication, I recommend that a new Division be created consisting
solely of the Lodges of Hawaii and that an appropriate number of Inspectors be appointed by the Grand Master to serve with a newly appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer of the Division so created . The decision
as to the number of Inspectors and who shall be appointed by the Grand
Master will be recommended by the Grand Lecturer after conferring with
the Ritual Committee and Executive Committee of Grand Lodge. This
will be accomplished by deleting the word "Six" from the second line of
Section 116, page 63 of the California. Masonic Code. I have confidence
that future Grand Masters with the aid of the Executive Committee, Grand
Lecturer and members of the Ritual Committee will administer this duty
well. I also believe the Brethren of Hawaii will use this wisely to determine
the future of Freemasonry in Hawaii. Like many of my predecessors I too
believe that the Grand Lodge of Hawaii is inevitable. The only question
is when and how. I further believe that the Special Committee's recommendations No. 2 and No. 3 should be tabled until this new Division has
been established and is functioning, in order that additional input be available for further study and voting. I believe a period of meditation is appropriate at this time. Those recommendations that should be tabled read
as follow:
2-That the edict by Grand Master Herbert Huebner, October 6,
1971 , prohibiting any activity on the part of the Masons in Hawaii
in the formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii , if still in force, be
terminated and that a committee of fifteen qualified representative
members of Hawaiian Lodges should be appointed to develop plans
and procedures for consideration of the formation of a Grand Lodge
of Hawaii.
J.-That the proposal to form a Grand Lodge of Hawaii should be
submitted to a vote of the membership of the Hawaiian Lodges at
an appropriate time after the committee has completed its tasks. The
method of voting and the interpretation of those votes must be detetmined in advance and be clearly understood by all participants.
In the event the proposal to form a Grand Lodge of Hawaii is rejected, the matter should not be reintroduced for a minimum period
of four years.
I wish to commend the members of the Special Committee for their fine
efforts. They are Past Grand Master Vernon L. Gordon, Chairman, Past
Grand Master Theodore Meriam, Worshipful Lee A. Strong and ex officio,
the two Inspectors William McKee and Oswald Lau.

I believe my original plan for using local Lodge officers and Inspectors in
the activities and in Grand Lodge ceremonies as much as possible has
manifested itself in giving each of them the thrill of being a real part of
Grand Lodge and rightfully so. It has been possible because of the willingness of the Appointive Grand Lodge Officers to attend events only in

RECOMMENDATIONS
The great honor and experience of serving as your 117th Grand Master
during the 134th year of our Grand Lodge has produced many observations
and thoughts. A banker by profession, I have been constantly aware of
the financial, administrative, and operational functions of our Grand
Lodge, and I have tried my best to act as Chairman of the Board and
Chief Executive Officer of this great corporation with assets in excess of
$125,000,000 and total budgets exceeding $11,000,000. However, all cannot be relegated to the cold glassy eye of the business executive for in the
heart of this Grand Lodge pumps the warm blood of fraternal love which
flows through the body made up of the Constituent Lodges and all our
dedicated Brethren. To them belongs this Grand Lodge and our programs
should be for them. Therefore, I have six recommendations to submit to
this Grand Body:

Number 2.-Term of Office of Inspectors
I recommend the term of appointment of Inspectors be on a calendar
year basis, January 1 through December 31. I believe this more closely

34

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

coincides with the term of office of the officers of most of the Lodges the
Inspector supervises and will enable him to make a more accurate assessment of each group of Lodge officers in his District in his annual report.
It also enables the Grand Master to make any changes he deems appropriate in the appointment of Inspectors three months following his installation rather than nine months, thus serving with them for nine months
instead of three months as now. To accomplish this I recommend changing
the last sentence of Section No. 1120 of the C.M.C. to read, "Commencing
on January 1st followng the Grand Master's Installation and terminating
on December 31 of the same year."

was nearly washed away by the torments of the mighty peaceful Pacific

for a "Lodge Disaster Relief Fund" to which the Brethren and Constituent
Lodges may be permitted to contribute for future emergencies, and a
report be presented for action of Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication.

Number 3.-0pti onal Use of a "Short Form" Closing Ceremony
Recognizing as I traveled throughout the Jurisdiction, that our Fraternity competes for the time of busy people and that some of our work can
become redundant and time consuming, and consequently does not really
accomplish its intent, I submit the following: I have observed the enthusiastic acceptance of the Grand Master's prerogative to close Grand Lodge
"in short form" thereby avoiding any anticlimax to the ceremony itself. I
believe it worthy of consideration that the Grand Lecturer and Ritual
Committee develop a "short form" closing ceremony to be used by Constituent Lodges of this Jurisdiction as an optional method of closing Lodge
at all Special Meetings only. The formal closing should still be required at
all Stated Meetings. The recommendation of the Grand Lecturer and Ritual Committee will be presented to this Grand Lodge in the form of a
Resolution for a vote of the members of Grand Lodge at the next Annual
Communication of this Grand Lodge.
Number 4-Tabl e Lodge Ceremony
In recent years many Constituent Lodges have used a "Table Lodge
Ceremony" as a means of fraternal fellowship as well as a social program
for their members.
Various rituals borrowed from other jurisdictions were used, even
though they were not specifically authorized by the Grand Lodge of California or its Ritual Committee. After much consideration by your Executive Committee, I requested our Ritual Committee to prepare a Table
Lodge Ceremony which might be adopted by this Grand Lodge, thus
standardizing the Ritual to be used by all Lodges in this Jurisdiction. Such
a ceremony has been prepared and is now available for use. When
adopted, we can then be assured that we all will be using the same ceremony for this Masonic program designed to promote fellowship in our
Lodges. I therefore recommend the Table Lodge Ceremony, as prepared
by the Ritual Committee, be adopted and printed in proper form for
distribution to the Constituent Lodges for their use as desired.

at the hands of Mother Nature. Kauai Lodge No. 589 and many of its

Number 6.-Moj ave Lodge No. 783
Much to my dismay and with some hesitancy, it was necessary for me
to arrest the charter of Mojave Lodge No. 783 in April of this year because
no qualified officers came forward. This was done after many discussions
with Worshipful Harold Macy, Inspector of the 504th Masonic District.
Worshipful Brother Hal had worked very closely and diligently in attempting to help the Brethren of Mojave Lodge either qualify as officers , consolidate with another Lodge or in some other manner save their Lodge,
but all to no avail. The members of the Lodge seemed to have no desire
to serve as officers ;md the Lodge refused to vote the necessary legislation
for consolidation. There are currently only seven or eight members out of
a membership which has constantly dropped to about 85, who are interested in helping the Lodge survive, but they do nothing but meet to discuss
the problem and do not take any positive action. It is, therefore, my
recommendation that the charter of Mojave Lodge No. 783 be revoked
acc0rding to sections 106 and 2106b of the California Masonic Code.
Other recommendations have been agreed on with the Grand Treasurer
and the Chairman of the Finance Committee on financial matters; with
the Grand Lecturer and Ritual Committee on Ritual, and with the Grand
Secretary on the operations of Grand Lodge but these do not require
legislation or Grand Lodge approval.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master recommends that a new Division be created comprised of the Lodges of Hawaii and that an appropriate number of Inspectors be appointed to serve with an Assistant Grand Lecturer of the
Division so created . He now further approves the second and third recommendations of the Special Committee with a caution as to the third
recomme ndatiol} .
The governance of the Lodges of Hawaii has been the subject of discussion for many years .
Most recently, Grand Master West discussed some of the history and
recommended appointment of a new special committee to study the feasibility of establishing a District G rand Lodge of Hawaii " under the auspices and subordinate to the Grand Lodge of Califo rnia."
The recommended Special Committee was appointed . It spent a great
deal of time and effort in dete rmining the sentiments fo r and against , the
reasons for and against , and effects to be accomplished by the concept
discussed by G rand Maste r West, as well as other possible alternatives.
The repo rt which it has made at this Annual Communication . recommended 1) the establishment of a new Division of the Grand Lodge ; 2)
that Grand Master Huebner's 1971 edict be declared rescinded and that a
Committee o f fifteen qualified representative members of Hawaiian
Lodges should be appointed to develop plans and procedures fo r consideration of the formation of a G rand Lodge of Hawaii;" and 3) that the
proposal to be made by that committee be submitted to a vote of the
membe rship of the Hawaiian Lodges at an appropriate time afte r the committee has made its proposal. It is the hope of Grand Master Maynard
that this step will be so delayed as to give an opportunity for the Division
concept to show its effectiveness.

It is these second and third recommendations that the Grnnd Master
also approves and recommends. The precise content of the second and
third parts of this recommendation are now fully set forth in the report of
the Special Committee.
The matter has been studied for long enough. Whatever may be the
next step in the progression of self-governance, it is now time for this step
to be taken.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee concurs in the Grand Master 's three-fold Recommendation and recommends a Yes vote.

To carry out the intent of the Grand Master, your Committee submits
the following legislation:
RESOLVED, that Section 1120 of the Califo rnia Masonic Code be
amended by deleting th e second sentence and substituting the following :
"Each Inspector shall serve for a term of one yea r, commenci ng o n
January 1st following the Grand Master's installatio n ."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption o f
the Resolution.

The Committee on Finance:

For some time prior to the 1972 Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge, the term of ofllce for Inspectors was, by custom. for the ca lendar
year following the Annual Communication.
.
At the 1972 Annual Communication the Grand Master recommended
that the term of office for Inspectors be changed to run concurrently with
that of the Grand Master. That change made the term of an Inspecto r the
same as that for all other Officers and Committeemen of the Grand Lodge,
including the Assistant Grand Lecturers.
However, at the 1973 Annual Communication the Grand Lecturer reported that the new term o f office was not beneficial and some problem
areas had been encountered when qualifications for Lodge Officers had to
be conducted by a newly appointed Inspector. At the Grand Lecturer's
recomme ndation the term of office for Inspecto rs was changed , by vote
of the Grand Lodge, to be from July 1 of each year to June 30 of the
following year.
Our present Grand Master has recommended that the term of office for
Inspectors be ch~nged to the system in effect prior to the 1972 Annual
Communication. That is, for the calendar year, January through December.
Since that system seemed to satisfy the needs of Grand Masters, the
Grand Lodge, and Constituent Lodges without undu e difficulty for many
years, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes approves the recommendation.
I, therefore, move that Grand Maste r's R ecomme ndation No. 2 be approved , and your committee recommends a "yes" vote.

The Committee on Finance, at the request of the Grand Master, has
included the amount of $10,000 in the proposed budget to cover expenses
of this new Division for the remainder of the year in the event of approval
of the recommendation.
Because a final plan of operation for the proposed new Division has not
been resolved, your Committee on Finance can only make rough estimates
of the additional costs required for the new activity.
Major cost items in the operation of this new Division will be the amount
of travel between the Mainland and Hawaii. The Finance Committee has
been informed that the tentative plans for operation of the new Division
contemplates only the very minimum of additional travel between the
Mainland and Hawaii by essential personnel, and therefore recommends
approval of the recommendation.

The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual commends the "Hawaii Study Committee''
for their very thorough in-depth study and conclusion to form a new Division.
Working with our Hawaiian Brethren these many years has been most
enjoyable, and we share in this happiness in the proposed Recommendation. We look forward to a closer relationship by the formation of an
additional Division.
We therefore concur most enthusiastically with the proposed Recommendation and urge an overwhelming "yes" vote.
The Grand Master's Recommendation was adopted.

RECOMMEN DATION No. 4

TABLE LODGE CEREMO NY

The Committee 011 Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Maynard's Annual Message sets forth a recommen dation
that the Table Lodge Ceremony , as prepared by the Ritual Committ~e, be
adopted and printed in proper form for distributio n to the Constituen t
Lodges for their use as desired.
.
.
. .
A Table Lodge Ceremony is held in an untiled room and 1s a nt~ahsttc
ceremony and suggested program for a Lodge to celebrate .. Maso~1c Fe~­
tivals" such as the Feasts of the Sts. John and to promote fellowship. It is
not to be attended by non-Maso ns.
Your Committe e on Policy and General Purposes has reviewed the proposed draft of the "Table Lodge Ceremony ." The document c?~tains the
history of such events, advance preparatio n of the Lodge dining room
including the arrangeme nt of the tables and seating of the Officers a.nd
Brethren . The guide or document continues with recommen ded entertainment , traditional toasts to be proposed with wording provided, recipes for
non-alcoholic punches and an opening and closing ritual.
Your Committe e on Policy and General Purposes believes that Grand
Lodge should control the acts of the Constitue nt Lodges as to ritual, accounting, etc, However, we arc concerned that the adoption. of the for~al
Table Lodge Cere mony moves into the realm of controlling the social
programs of a Lodge. Your Co mmittee can foresee the time when poss~bly
a ritual and scenerio for a Widow's Pin Ceremony or Layman's Night
would be mandated .
Therefore , your Committe e on Policy and General Purposes believes
that as a guideline for those Lodges desiring to participate in a Table Lodge
Ceremony , the proposed ceremony will accomplish the inte nt and ~an b.c
printed without approval of Grand Lodge . However, your Committe e ts
concerned that such a fellowship program not become an edict of this
Grand Lodge and therefore we recommen d a "No" vote on the formal
adoption of the Tahle Lodge Ceremony as a ceremony of Grand Lodge.
The Committee on Ritual:
At the request o f our Grand Master and the Executive Committe e. the
Ritual Committe e has prepared a Table Lodge Ce remony, titled " The
Table Lodge of Fellowship ." It is now ready f~r your considerati.on: .
At the present time, Table Lodge Ceremoni es from other 1unsd1ct1ons
are not permitted in California . Although the Ritual Committe e has ?ffered some guidelines , in the past , for a Table Lodge Program , a cons1d-

LODGE DISASTE R RELIEF F UND

The Committee 011 Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master's Recomme ndation No. 5 seeks to have the incoming
Grand Maste r appoint a Special Committe e to study the fcasihility of
setting up a Special Fund to be established within our Grand Lodge for a
"Lodge Disaster Relief Fund."
The Fund would receive donations from the Constituen t Lodges and
individual Brothers. The purpose of the Fund would be to help Lodges in
our Jurisdictio n in future emergencies such as destruction by earthquak es
and other natural disasters .
Your Committe e on Policy and General Purposes be lieves that such a
study would be proper and helpful.
Therefore , I move approval of Recomme ndation No. 5 and recommend
a " Yes" vote.

Section 2116 of the California Maso nic Code requires for forfe iture of
the Charter of a constituent Lodge , that charges against the Lodge shall

charges the Lodge accused shall have had due no tice.
A continuing course of eve nts o ver the last 2 1 months constitutes substantial com pliance with this Section .

Recommendation .

Lodge No. 783 a nd recommends that the Charter be revoked by Grand
Lodge due to failure of the Lodge and its members to provide qualified
Office rs to carry o n the business of the Lodge.

under the existing circu m stances occurring in Mojave Lodge No. 783 the
Grand Master had no alternative but to arrest the charter and recommeml
revocation thereof by G rand Lodge. Your Policy and General Purposes
Committee therefore recommends a favorable vote o n Grand Master's
Recommendation Numbe r 6.

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful G rand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
As prescribed in our Law, an examination of o ur June 30, 1983 financial
statements was conducted by Lindquist. von Husen and Joyce, Certified
Public Accountants . San Francisco.
Their complete reports are a n integra l part of this Grand Treasurer's
report which will be found in the final printed Proceedings of this Communication. Pre -printed copies of these re ports are supplied to a ll Lodge
representati ves attending this Annual Communica tion. and. as usual , we
urge your attention.
At our Annua l Communica tion two years ago, we informed you of the
need to adopt accrual accounting methods, the replacement of an aged
bookkeepin g mac hine with a mini computer system and a search fo r more
competent accounting personnel.
All this became an accomplishe d fact during the past fiscal year. Our
Accounting staff is now furnishing accurate and timely financial data to all
Boards, to our Executive Committee, and to our Finance and other Grand
Lodge committees.
It continues to be a distinct pleasure to serve Grand Lodge as your
Grand Treasure r. Sincere appreciation is extended to the Elective Line ,
our Grand Secretary, and to all o ur dedicated Grand Lodge employees for
their cheerful assistance.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN A . SICKENBERGE R. Grand Treasurer

Referred to the Committee on Distribution . T he Committee on Distribution referred the entire report to the Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:
In accordance with the regulations of our Grand Lodge, I herewith
present my annual report, relating to ritual, as regards the various Lodges
in this Jurisdiction , ascertained by some personal visitation, correspondence and reports of the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts.
RITUAL MEETINGS, CONFERENCES AND SEMINARS

Ritual Committee meetings were held to discuss and take action on the
many inquiries placed with the Grand Lecturer in regard to ritual, protocol
and administration. In addition , instruction and exemplification in our
ritual were held for the benefit of our Assistant Grand Lecturers. These
meetings were held October 29, 30, 1982 in Fresno; January 20 prior to
our Conference in Ontario; June 3. 4, 5, 1983 in Ontario; and September
9, 10. 11 in Sacramento. Committee meetings were also held in conjunction
with the Annual Spring Conferences, as follow:
Division I

February 18-20 in Santa Rosa conducted by the
W:. Donald E. Weisse.
Division II
April 15-17 in Sacramento conducted by the
W:. Louis A. Lasell, Sr.
March 18-20 in Los Gatos conducted by the
Division III W:. Ulysses G. Patropulos.
Division IV May 20-22 in Bakersfield conducted by the
W:. William J. Taylor.
June 17-19 in Lancaster conducted by the
Division V • W:. Philip I. Hylton.
Division VI- January 21-23 in Ontario conducted by the
W:. Morton B. Glick.

Seminars were held by the Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors.
These seminars are important to the continuance of good ritual throughout
the Jurisdiction. They were well attended and very well received.
LODGES

Dissemination of the Inspectors· reports informs us that one of every
four serving in the top three chairs of the Lodges are Past Masters. 25%.
This indicates the unwillingness of many of our members to undertake the
obligation of serving their Lodge as an officer.
Ritual proficiency rating of officers is reasonably good, but for the first
time, reports indicate over 1% in the poor category. This is an area of
immediate concern for all of us , everyone in this Jurisdiction. It has not
been condoned in the past, nor should it be in the future.
Funeral Certificate holders in this Jurisdiction number approximately
1,809. An average of 2.9 for every Lodge. Our concern in this area should
be that 77 of o ur Lodges have absolutely no certificate holders and another

Candidate coaching is still an area of concern for all of us. Apparently,
our reports o n this subject have had no effect o n the Lodges. We have
recomme nded more aggressiveness on the part of the Candidates Coach.
Right Wo rshipful Roy Henville has made a study that indicates we now

ago this was o nly 1 out of 100. Many things must be wrong . We evidently
arc not impressing these candidates with th e performance of our ritual.
the beauties of Free masonry, or the things that brought each of us back.
Perhaps our Candidates Coaches are not doing their job. Perhaps they are
waiting for the candidate to come to them. Perhaps these coaehes are not
informed well enough to explain to them the impo rtance and the beauties
of o ur teachings. Rhetoric is not the answer. Impressio ns are. The importance of the Candidates Coach and his impressions upon the candidate are
as importa nt as any thing we have to offer. Masters and Wardens of this
Grand Lodge, these responsibilities fall with you. If o ur Fraternity is to
survive, I must stress to you the importance of this aspect of o ur Fraternity.

GRAND LODGE RITU AL

This assemblage, at the last Annual Communication, approved the recommendation of Most Wo rshipful Robert 0. West. that the Institution and
Constitution Ceremonies be made public ceremonies. This was immediately accomplished and Most Worshipful Harry L. Maynard was enabled
to Constitute Half Moo n Bay Lodge two days after his installation. and
Kona Lodge on July 23, 1983. I am happy to report that these changes
have been received by the general public with an overwhelming amount
of acceptanee. Those of you who participated in the vote to make this
happen are to be congratulated.
HAWAIIAN MASONRY

Mid-July was chosen as our ritual visit to th at paradise in the Paeific , in
o rder to attend and assist our Grand Master with the Constitution of o ur
ne west Lodge.
Schools of instruction were held and the work was exemplified . Interest
and eagerness to do the work prope rly, by a large majority of the Lodges,
was very evident .
As stated last year. o ur Lodges of the 50th State arc having many of the
same proble ms that plague our Mainland Lodges. Lack of officer material ,
Past Masters tilling stations. lack of petitions for membership , and too
many me mbe rs that do no t reside near their Lodge. Many of their memhe rs reside on the Mainland.
As I have reported before, our Island Inspectors. Ozzie Lau and Bill
McKee are doing great work under the most difficult of circumstances.
They are not offered the same amount of instruction as that received by
our Mainland lnspectors, due to the great distances between the Islands

INSPF.CTORAL CORPS

The duties of the Inspectors are set forth in Sectio n 1122 of the California Masonic Code. Howeve r, over the years additio nal duties and hurdens have been added to their responsibilities and, as the Grand Maste r's
represe ntative in the District to whieh he is assigne d, his activities cover
a broad spectrum of authority. This hardy band of dedicated Masons has
done yeoman work throughout our Jurisdiction , year after year, and this
year has been no exception. With each passing year, in addition to already
prescribed duties, the Inspector is charged with the respo nsibilities of arrange ments for the increasing number of Grnnd Lodge ceremonies, reeeptions fo r the Grand Master, and other speeial meetings in which Grand
Lodge is involved. Their's is an indispensable service to Masonry and no
praise is too great for their unselfish contributio ns of time and talent to
o ur great Fraternity and its work.
To those of the Corps who have chosen retirement during the year, I
wish to offer a sincere thank you on behalf of the Grand Lodge and the
Ritual Committee for your untiring efforts o n o ur behalf and for the benefit of o ur Fraternity. It is indeed a pleasure to welcome the new Inspectors
who have received their appointments this year, and we will be loo king
forward to wo rking wit h each of you.
FUNERAL SERVICE

As I stated in my last report, Funeral Certifi cate holders ; in this Jurisdiction, was an area of deep concern by our committee. And one of the
highest priorities in the coming year wo uld be a study of this subject , with
some possible recommenda tio ns and revisions to a lleviate the problem.
It was brought to the attention of the committee this past December by
our Grand Secretary, that the supply of Funeral Services was nearing depletio n . We have been working o n an improved version for well over a
yea r. Included in this revision arc the followi ng:

l. The book has been divided into three separate ceremonies. Ritu al
fo r Chapel, Home, Church, Synagog.ue or Graveside Service . Ritual
for Lodge Room and Lodge Room Memo rial Service. Ritual for
Memo rial Service other than Lodge R oom Memo rial Service. Wording of the three services is exactly the sa me, however. being separated, mo re elearly defines the various aspects involved.
2. Forewords for each ceremony have been included in the appropriate
place.
3. Instructions for movements and options have been located immediately in front of the appropriate ritual and will be printed in red,
just as our Installation Ceremony has used for a numbe r of years.

5. Certification of officiant has also been incorporated.
6. An index to each section has been provided.
This revision will provide those unfamiliar with our ceremony. a much
easier method in learning and understanding the various deliveries. No
more footnotes. No more going to the back of the book and then to the
front to locate a specific instruction.
We have made absolutely no change in ritual or in movement options.
Our only desire in preparing these revisions, is to make the book more
efficient. Other than the book being thicker than that used previously. we
believe you will find it much easier to use. Copies of this book will he
printed and ready for distribution as soon as possible.
RECOMMENDATION

It became apparent to me, immediately upon beginning my tenure in
office 2 years ago. that we were having a multitude of problems with
respect to the Funeral Service and its delivery.
Brother Arthur R. Kirk, Chairman of the Masonic Service Bureaus,
related to me many areas of concern. While 1 have no intention of burdening the members of this Grand Lodge with the details of these concerns. this subject became the number one priority of the Ritual Committee. It was a topic of discussion at each and every meeting.
At the 1970 Annual Communication and under the direction of Past
Grand Master, Chester R. MacPhee, a program of certification was
adopted by the Ritual Committee, which provided the present system of
Funeral Certificate proficiency. Thanks are due Most Worshipful MacPhee
for his astuteness in recognizing the extreme gravity of the situation and
his determination in helping to remove this blemish from the face of Masonry.
This program has been in effect since that time and worked very well
for a number of years after its inception. However, the system is now very
much in need of fortification.
Masters of our Constituent Lodges. as a requirement for qualification,
have been required to be proficient in our Funeral Service . This has ofttimes resulted in hardship on this particular individual. It has also caused
Inspectors to qualify certain individuals with weaknesses and instabilities
in the performance of our Funeral Service. It has provided those Masters.
who may not be qualified in the proper delivery. to feel justified in the
performance of the Service.
I submit to you that anything our Fraternity docs, when it comes to an
offering in Public, especially at a time of bereavement. must be done by
the best we have to give and not by anyone only partially qualified . Our
C.M.C. is.also sketchy as to who is qualified to deliver the Service. The
only reference to the program of certification. at the present time. is to be
found in the Inspector 's Manual.
It is therefore my recommendation, that the following program he
adopted as the requirement for certification and that Section 2908 be re-

89

CERTIFICATION FOR MASON IC' FUNERAL SERVICE

1. No Bro~her ~Master, Past Master or any other Brother) shall perform
the California Masonic Funeral Service without being properly certified. (CMC 2908, Supp .)
2. The Inspector of the District shall certify to the proficiency of all who
perform the Funeral Service for the Lodges within his District. or·
those of adjacent Districts. The Inspector shall, upon being completely satisfied as to the proficiency and qualification of such Brot hers, forward to the Grand Master a request that a certificate of qualification and authorization be issued which shall grant said Brother
the authority to perform the California Masonic Funeral Service
when properly requested to do so.
3. Prior to officiating, the Master must be certified in the Funeral Service. If the Master is not certified. it shall be the responsibility of the
Master and the Inspector to have a certified Brother available at all
times.
4. In order to qualify, the following requirements must be demonstrated
by the Brother to the complete satisfaction of the Inspector:
a. Delivery of the Funeral Service in its entirety in a creditable manner. With some Brothers this may require total memorization; others may be able to read and deliver it in a creditable manner.
b. Proper pfonunciation and enunciation.
c. Complete knowledge of duties and responsibilities of Funeral Service Officiant.
d. Personal habits. dignity and appearance appropriate to the solemnity of the Service.
e. Emotional stability.
5. All requests for certificates shall be submitted o n the Grand Lodge
form to be furni shed to the Inspector and shall be effective for a
period of three years from date of issuance.
6. Inspector shall maintain a current record of all qualified Brethren in
his District. with date of certification and expiration date and shall
forward a copy to the Grand Lecturer and Assistant Grand Lectu re r
on July 1, each year. when filing his annual report.
7. Inspector shall furnish to the Master of each Lodge in his District
and the Executive Secretary of all adjacent Masonic Service Bureaus.
a written list of all Brothers who are currently qualified in his District
each year. He shall also notify the above named individuals of any
additions or deletions during the year, at the time such changes shall
occur.
8. Prior to renewal of any certificate, the Inspector must satisfy himself
as to the Brother's proficiency.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
To th e Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board is pleased to submit its 5lst
Annual Report covering the fiscal year ending June 30. 1983. The members
of our great Fraternity have o nce again expressed their love an d concern
for the residents o f o ur two Homes by their contributions to the Endowment Fund which have exceeded one million dolla rs.
INCOME FRO!'.f THE PERMANENT ENDOWMENT FUND

Income from the Permanent Endowment Fund amounted to $4,238,680.99
which amount was transferred to the operating account of our two Ho mes.
This income is an extremely and vitally important factor in providing the
Homes Trustees with the funds necessary to maintain the quality of care
afforded to the residents of both of our Homes .

Respectfully submitted .

REPORT OF THE CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
PUBLICATION BOARD
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
California Freemason is the official publication of the Grand Lodge. Its
quarterly publication and distribution is administered by a board composed
of the Grand Master. the Grand Secretary and an Editor-in-Chief appointed by the Grand Master.
The magazine is now in its 30th consecutive year of puhlication . Mo re
than 800.000 copies were mailed to members of California Lodges, to paid
subscribers . and to other Grand Jurisdictions throughout the United States
and the world. The magazine is often quoted in Masonic journals in foreign
countries .
The object of the magazine is to maintain strong lines of communication
~tween the Grand Lodge and the members of Ca lifornia Lodges. Within
Its pages, Lodges have the opportunity to announce Hiram and Golden

Veteran Awards. Articles are published pertaining to Widows Nights, Layman's Nights, community activities of Lodges, Constitution and Public
Schools Observance programs, and the laying of cornerstones by Grand
~~.

.

.

.

.

.

California Freemason features articles and stones of histo ric m~erest,
especially relating to California's rich heritage and tradition .. F~om ttme to
time articles of outstanding merit published in other Masonic Journals are
reprinted in the magazine. The reader :an be kept well informed of Freemasonry's activities throughout the Umted States and t~e world.
No commercial advertising is accepted by the magazine, but the operations of the Masonic Homes of California and the activities of the ir residents are publicized. Scholarship awards by the California Masonic Foundation are announced in every issue together with photographs of the
. .
recipients.
An annual subscription to the magazine is only $4.00 and 1s highly recommended as a gift to friends, neighbors and relatives. It ~ffers an excellent way to keep others informed of the charitable , educational ~nd beneficial programs conducted by the world's largest and oldest fraternal
o rder.

MORNING SESSION-T uesday, October 11, 1983
At 9:00 A.M. the Grand Lodge was called on, the Grand Master presiding . Grand Lodge was raised by Ernest B. Rider. Jr. . A Past Master
and Charter Master of Orange County Daylight Lodge No. 833 and Vandell C. Owen, C harter Master of Square and Compass Lodge No. 834 ,
using the gavel presented to the Grand Master at the Open Constitutio n
Ceremony for Half Moon Bay Lodge No. 835. Other gavels used by the
Grand Master during the Morning Session were presented to him by the
610th Masonic District at a re ception in Glendora ; a mounted gavel presented at the Constitution of Square and Compass Lodge No. 834 in Chino ;
at a 75 year Veterans Award Presentation to Chester B. Neiswender by
Perris Lodge No. 411 at Sun City; a gavel presented by Woodrow C.
Cavanaugh , Grand Lodge Representative to Japan in Los Angeles; 75th
Anniversary of University Lodge No. 394 in Torrance ; a Reception given
by the 608th Masonic District in Whittier; the Long Beach Area Maste rs
and Wardens A ssociation Reception for the Grand Master in Lakewood;
at a Breakfast Reception by the Orange County 635th Masonic District in
Santa Ana; the Cornerstone Ceremony for San Bernardino Government
Center by the Lodges of the 602nd District in San Bernardino ; a Cornerstone Ceremony for the Anaheim Masonic Temple in Anaheim by Anchor
Lodge No. 273; Anaheim Lodge No. 207, Mother Colony Lodge No. 750
and Azure Lodge No. 533.
The Invocation wtis delivered by the Very Reverend Sidney S. Guthman,
Grand Chaplain. Minutes of the Morning and Afternoon Sessions of Monday, October 10, 1983 were approved as read by the Grand Secretary.

Grand Lodge was called off at 4:45 P. M . to be called on again at 9:00
A. M. on Tuesday, October 11, 1983.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTE E ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureau s is pleased to submit its
Annual Report on the operations and condition of the nineteen Masonic
Service Bureaus for the year ending June 30, 1983 . The Committee is on
its 56th year.
The Right Worshipful E . Arthur Haglund, Deputy Grand Master, was
appointed liaison officer and we have appreciated his support and assistance during the year.
T~e Committee is well aware of its responsibility in directing the operatton of the Bureaus in a uniform manner. The Service Bureaus assist
the sojourners , their widows and orphans, operate blood banks , arrange
and conduct funerals for deceased Masons, make investigations, assist in
the applications for the Masonic Homes, visit sick and promote fraternal
relations with sojourners.
