form 199 or 199B. The Los Angeles Bureau prepares forms other than
the 990 and the 199. All Bureaus that require tax returns have filed them
on schedule.

We welcome to our Committee as its new member. Delmer W. May, a
Past Master of Magnolia Lodge No. 242 of Santa Barbara . He served as
Executive Secretary of the Santa Barbara Bureau for a twenty-five yeaI
period.
NEW EXECUTIVE SECRETARIES

We welcome Edward Levitt who assumed the duties of Secretary of the
Glendale Bureau following the resignation of John E . Harney. Stanley C.
Cory assumed the duties of Secretary of San Gabriel Bureau following the
resignation of James E. Graham. John A. McGuish assumed the duties of
Secretary of the Santa Monica Bureau following the resignation of Harry
W. Flanders. A. W. Grandstaff assumed the duties of Secretary of the San
Jose Bureau following the resignation of Jay W. Robinson.
MEETINGS

The Committee he ld four meetings during the year. One was held during
Grand Lodge Weck. At that time the officers and representatives of many
Bureaus met with the Committee.
A regional meeting was held in Oakland on February 26, 1983. Thirtythree officers of the Bureaus located in Northern California attended the
meeting.
A regional meeting was held in Los Angeles on March 26. 1983. Thirtytive officers and representatives located in Southern California attended
the meeting. At both the Northern and Southern California meetings the
Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger. Grand Secretary. was the guest
speaker. His message of Masonry in California was well received.
A meeting was held in Santa Barbara on June 14, 1983 to review the
Budgets of the Bureaus and to conduct other Committee business.
UNIFORM COMPACTS

As the result of the consolidation of Lodges , new Uniform Compacts
have been approved by the Grand Master with Golden Gavel Lodge No.
445, Norwalk Lo dge No. 315 , with the Los Angeles Bureau.
Redondo Lodge No. 328, Downey Lodge No. 220. Jewell City Lodge
No. 652. Glendale Lodge No. 544 and La Canada-Oakwood Lodge No.
739 are all new members of the Los Angeles Bureau .
As the result of consolidation of Lodges. a new Uniform Compact was
approved by the Grand Master for Fountain Valley Lodge No. 351 with
the Orange County Bureau.
Orange County Daylight Lodge No. 833 is a new member of the Orange
County Bureau.
TAXES

All Bureaus have filed the required information return to the Internal
Revenue Service on Form 990 and the State Franchise Tax Board on either

149

BUDGETS

Each Bureau presents a Budget for the approval of the Committee on
or before th~ first of May each year. The Budget covers the opernting
expense and income for the penod starting July 1st and ending June 30th.
The Budget recommends a per capita assessment to be collected from their
member Lodges.
The approved Budgets covering the operation of the Bureaus decreased
over the past year to a total estimated expense of $134,685.
BUSH MASONIC RELIEF

The Worshipful Ralph H. Head , President of the Bush Masonic Relief
and the Trustees provide the operating funds for the Bureaus located in
the Greater Los Angeles Area. The contributions amounted to 68% of
the total Budgets for the eighteen Bureaus. The Masters. officers and
members of the Lodges join with the members of our Committee in expressing appreciation to the Trustees of the Bush Masonic Relief for their
generous contribution for the operation of the Bureaus in the Greater Los
Angeles Arca.
GLENDALE B U REAU

Effective July 1, 1983 the operation of the Glendale Bureau was discontinued_. The remaining four Lodges joined the Los Angeles Bureau.
The remammg assets of the Bureau were distributed to the three Masonic
Youth Groups.
MASONIC RELIEF ASSOCIATION OF TH F. U. S. AND CANADA

Our Grand Lodge now holds membership in the Masonic Relief Assoc.iatio~ of th~ United States ~nd Canada . The Association has many func-

t10ns including the correlation of the various forms of Masonic relief
throughout the United States and Canada . Our California Bureaus will
benefit from this membership.
We are pleased to report that the Executive Secretary of the Los Angeles
Bureau , Lloyd V. Smith. is a Director of the A ssociation .
ANNUAL REPORTS

. All Bureaus have supplied the annual reports to the Committee. They
include_ the Election Report, Budget, Statistical and Financial Report,
Operatmg Expenses and Fixed Assets as well as the Blood Bank report.
. The Bureaus conducted 477 Masonic Funeral Services for deceased soJOu_rners, made 380 visits to sick sojourners. and conducted 276 investigations. The Executive Secretaries of the Bureaus assisted in preparing 61

Although the maintenan ce of our edifice requires a continued expenditure of monies. your Trustees are pleased to report that we are still able
this year to donate $40.000.00 to the Masonic Homes Endowme nt Fund,
in accordanc e with our By-Laws.
The California Masonic Memorial Temple serves several no ble functions. In previous years we have indicated the broad spectrum of community involveme nt rep resented hy the functions which are held in our
auditorium . This year they included :

To The Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masoni1: Memo rial Temple
hereby su bmics its 28th annual report.
At the close of the 1982 Annual Communi cation of Grand Lodge. the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its
organizati onal meeting as required by the California Maso nic Code. nominating and electing the following officers for the ensuing year :

The California Masonic Memorial Temple serves as a patriotic mo nument and memorial , open to the public, commemo rating the members of
the armed services of the United States and of the Most Worshipfu l Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California . who gave
their Jives in battle during World War II. With this definition in mind. it
is ineumbent upon the Trustees to maintain the facility and to permit it to
function within the spirit associated with an historic monumen t of great
Masonic significance . The Trustees can report with confidence that all
those persons associated with the operation and maintenan ce of the California Masonic Memorial Temple have faithfully discharged their duties.
During the course of this year, the Trustees completed the update of all
previous policies relative to the Masonic Memorial Te mple and i~s prnperties. We now have at our fingertips a refer ence document that will assist
us in navigating our daily transactio ns along the cour~e set by the G rand
Lo dge .
In complianc e with our policy. the Trustees and Temple staff ha~~ ma_de
ongoing physical inspectio ns of the premises and the garage fac1ht1es, tn·
eluding audits of the garage o perations. We are in th e process of re_-evaluating the mai ntenance and rental parameter s of our rental properties on
Pinc Street.
We completed the maintenan ce work on the sound and lighting syste~
and a portion of the necessary resto ration of the marhle. We arc now tn
the process of re painting and doing some structural repairs in the garage.
along with a continuati on of marhlc restoration .
Of major significa nce to our operation was the negotiatio n of a n e~v
lease with Metro politan Parking Systems which was consum.ma ted t~1s
year. We have hig h expectatio ns th at the new arrangeme nt will he satisfactory not o nly for the Temple. hut also for the lessee. and all of the
patrons who will be utilizing the facilities in th e future .
The Trustees are pleased to announce the continuati on of last year's
policy of providing free parking to our de legates during the official transactions of Grand Lodge at th e Annual Communi cation.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To The Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California :
The 1983 Masonic year was a gratifying o ne for the Committe e on Charters. At our Annual Communi cation last year four Lodges were granted
Charters and numbers were assigned to each.

159

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CAUFORN!A

On October 15 , 1982 Half Moon Bay Lodge No. 835 w~s presented its
Charter by the Most Worshipful Harry L. Maynard . The ceremony was
beautifully performed a nd well attended.
On Saturday morning , November 13, 1982 Grand Lodge was opened in
the Garden Grove Masonic Temple for the purpose of presenting a Charter
to Orange County Daylight Lodge No. 833. The Lodge room was filled
for this auspicious occasion. In the evening Grand Lodge convened in
Chino for the presentation of a charter to Square and Compass Lodge No.
834. The Most Worshipful Harry L. Maynard presided at both ceremonies
which made for another outstanding Mason ic day.
July 23, 1983 stands out as the highlight of the year for me because on
that afternoon a Charter was presented to Kona Lodge No. 836 followed
by a magnificent luau. The ceremony culminated a week of the famous
Hawaiian hospitality for which our Island Brothers are so well known. I
am most grateful for being invited to participate in these events.
While I regret to report that no new Lodges applied for Dispensations
this year, I am pleased to notify you that King Kalakaua Masonic Club
has completed all preliminary steps and we should have their application
soon to become a Daylight Lodge in Honolulu which will bring to twelve
the number of Lodges in the State of Hawaii.
Inquiries have also been received from Orange County regarding the
formation of a new Research Lodge. We would encourage both groups to
continue in their efforts.
That portion of the Grand Secretary's Report dealing with charter
changes has been referred to the Committee on Charters.
Four Lodges have applied for changes of meeting place:
Alamo Lodge No. 122-Walnut Creek to Lafayette
Hermann Lodge No. 127-San Bruno to Burlingame
Anchor Lodge No. 273-Bellflower to Anaheim
Tustin Lodge No. 828-Tustin to Santa Ana
The following Lodges have consolidated during the past year:
Fellowship Lodge No. 290 and Garvanza Lodge No. 492, effective
November 3, 1982, to he known as Fellowship Lodge No. 290.
Larchmont Lodge No. 614 and Atwater Lodge No. 622, effective December 1, 1982, to be known as Atwater Larchmont Lodge No. 6 14.
Temple City Lodge No. 612 and Camellia Lodge No. 805, effective
December I, 1982, to be known as Camellia Lodge No. 612.
Albany Lodge No. 686 and E l Cerrito Lodge No. 705, effective December 6, 1982 , to be known as E l Cerrito-Albany Lodge No. 686.
Alpha Lodge No. 431 a nd Shattuck-Steph ens Lodge No. 541, effective
December 7, 1982 , to be known as Alpha Shattuck-Steph ens Lodge No.
431.
Argonaut-Argo nne Lodge No. 461 and Alta Vista-Mount Vernon
Lodge No. 464, effective April 4, 1983, to be known as Columbia Lodge
No. 461.
Verdugo Hills- Unity Lodge No. 368 and Meridian Lodge No. 667
and Frank S. La nd Lodge No. 819. effective April 5, 1983. to be known
as Jewel City Lodge No. 368.

Torra nce Lodge No. 447 a nd Rollin g Hills Lodge No. 781, effective
Septembe r 7, 1983 , to be known as Torrance Lodge No. 447.
Madera Lodge No. 280 and Joppa Lodge No. 508. effective September
13, 1983. to be known as Madera-Joppa Lodge No. 280.

Once again we thank you for the privilege and honor of serving our

REPORT OF THE INVESTMENT COMMITTE E
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Com mittee is pleased to submit its annual report on the
condition of the various funds of Grand Lodge and its entities. The committee meets quarterly during the yea r with its investme nt counselor. At
each meeting an independent investment organization presents a review
of the performance of the funds on a comparative basis with comparable
funds.
The Investment Committee recognizes the importance of diligent supervising of the in vestment of the funds of Grand Lodge. Three fund s, the
Masonic Hornes Endowment Fund, the Masonic Homes General Fund
and the Hugo M. Lorber Union City Home Fund constitute 97% of the
total investments.
The Investme nt Committee supervises other Grand Lodge funds: Grand
Lodge General Fund, California Masonic Memorial Temple. California
Masonic Foundation and Amaranth Fund, the Pooled Income Fund and
eighteen restricted-use funds for the Masonic Homes.
The marke t value of the total portfolio was $112.283.000 compared with
$84,710,000 a year earlier. The 1982-83 ann ual yield from the total invested
funds was 9.42%.
Government and corporate bonds and other fixed income securities
composed 76.6% of the tota l portfolio. Commo n stocks and convertible
bonds constituted the remainder.

REPORT OF THE COMMIT TEE ON COMMERCIALISM
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A . M. of California:
The Masonic Year 1982- 1983 has been a quiet one for this committee.

Our committee has been asked to investigate the unauthorize d useage of
the Square and Compass. All cases we re settled satisfacto rily.
This committee has also been d ealing with the issue of what fund raising
e ve nt is permissable for Masonic Lodges and the concordant bodies to
hold . Much e ffort has been spent reviewing the various proposals in light
of the guidance as set forth in the Appendix of and Pocke t Supplement to
the California Masonic Code. These two references give the event planner
guidance as to : I. Advertising ; 2. Public support; 3. Solicitatio n of gifts;
4. Commercial ventures; 5. Door prizes; 6. Gambling.

163

Each event planner should feel free to consult with the Committee on
Commercial ism. We will be happy to assist you to sec your even t is planned
and conducted according to the California Masonic Code.
Respectively submitted,
SHERWOOD C. KINGSLEY, Chairman

In the several meetings of the Committee held during the past year, the
primary thrust of our planning efforts were directed toward Constitution
Observance programmin g which would involve th e non-Masons of the
community as well as the membership of our Masonic Lodges located
there in. It was distressingly painful to learn from our discussions and from
correlating the reports received from Constituent Lodges, that a significant
numbe r were schepuling th e ir C onstitution Observance s only for the benefit of .their Masonic membership - an intolerable situation made even
mo_re intolerable in the realization that at least so me of these Lodges
believe that they are complying with the spirit of the Annual Proclamatio ns
issued by o ur Grand Masters.
This Committee is resolved to rectify this deplorable arrangeme nt
throu~h _a closer rel a tionship with the Maste rs and Wardens whose Lodges
are within the reasonable reac h of Committeem en. and through the va lued
assistance of our Masonic Inspectors in those areas where the Committee
is without proper representati on.
To accomplish this resolve , the Committee initiated the following actio n:
Updated an already excellent booklet , U. S. Constitution Observance
Guidelines, which contains many and varied ideas and suggestions
planning, prepa ring. and scheduling aggressive and meaningful programs.
Prepared sample news releases for publicizing observances .
Composed sample le tt e rs for corresponde nce with local government al
officials.
Drew up sample Constitution Observance Proclamatio ns for the co nvenience of local city and/or county leade rs.

important to maintain our Maso nic visibility in all our public undertakings.
Our dut y. as we perceive it. is to remind the people - to make the m more
aware - that they owe their well-being . their rights. their privileges. their
freedom. to the guarantees provided by the Constitution of the United
States - even their right and privilege to disagree with it o~ o_ccasio.n.
But. in reminding them. we should let them know that the maionty of Its
illustrious frame rs were Freemasons. and that it is the Freemasons of the
communitv who are behind its annual celebrations.

GRAND ORATION
"CAN YOUR SIGNATURE BE READ WITHOUT
THE USE OF SPECTACLES?"
RICHARD L. RIEMER , Grand Orator
Most Worshipful Grand Master, my Fellow Grand Lodge Officers, Past
Grand Masters. Distinguished Guests, Members of the Grand Lodge , my
Brethren All:
"Thank God! I- I also-am an American!"
With these stirring words of Daniel Webster as a backdrop. join me,
please . for a short journey through history.
It i.s the night of December the sixteenth, 1773 and. in Boston, St.
Andrews Lodge is about to hold its regularly scheduled meeting. But there
are only five members present that evening-one looks about the meeting
room at ~he famous Green Dragon Tavern and observes that mcin y of the
most active members of St. Andrew's are missing . Joseph Warren is not
in his usual chair, nor is John Hancock. Samuel Adams, Samuel Peck.
Paul Revere, and others. If you were to ask o ne of the five members who
were present , where their Brethren were. it is possible that you wo uld
h~ve seen a sly smile on his face and, with a twinkle in his eye, his response
might have been that they had a party to attend that evening.
And, yes, a p~rty_ did take place-the world's biggest tea party-as a
group of men , d1sgu1sed , more or less. as Indians, proceeded to Griffin's
Wharf, boarded the three British ships moored there. and filled Boston
harbor with their cargoes of tea.
My Brethren . I ask you, if such a cause existed today a nd such an event
was planned. would you be at the party?
The date is now April 18, 1775 , and General Gage of the British Army
has sent a d_etachment of ' 'regulars" to capture or destroy military stores
at Concord JUSt north of Boston. But the plan was suspected by the Minute
Men and our Brother, Paul Revere, awaited a signal to tell him of the
route the British were taking. Longfellow tells us in his famous poem.
" He said to his friend , 'If the British march
By land or sea from the town tonight
Hang a lantern aloft in the belfry arch
Of the North C hurch tower as a signal light.One, if by land. and two if by sea;' "
And the signal w~s given- two lanterns lit up the belfry at the Old
North Church-and Paul Revere, on a horse borrowed for that purpose.
rode through the countryside alerting his neighbors and the greater part
of the stores at Concord were saved.
~y Brethren , if today were the day and riders were needed. would yo u
be tn the saddle?
Jt is now June 16_. 1775, and the Past Grand Master and General Joseph
Warren togeth e_r wit~ our _Brother. General Israel Putna m. gathered with
some 1500 patnots, mcludmg many members of our Fraternity, to defend
Breed's Hill near Cambridge.

PROCEE DINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

The next da y the hattle took place-m isnamed the Battle of Bunker
Hill-and the 1500 Americans were attacked hy some 3000 British troops.
Waiting until they could see the whites of the enemies eyes, the inexperienced colonists delivered such a withering fire that the British line broke
in disorder. A second assault was mounted with a similar result and it was
not until the third assault that the British troops gained their objective and
then only after suffering the loss of 1054 men killed or wounded i.nciuding
some 89 commissioned officers. The defenders Jost some 420 killed and
wounded and 30 prisoners. Among the dead, however , was our Brother
Joseph Warren and, amo ng the wounded . was Brother Ephraim Kirby who

My Brethren , if that battle were to be fought today. would you be in

The date is August 2, 1776, and around a table in the Statehou se in
Philadelphia-the building now known as Indepe ndence Hall-are gathered the members of the Continental Congress who had. just one month
before, on July 2. 1776, adopted the resolutio n for independ ence. Two
days later, on July 4, 1776, the actual text of our Declarati on of Independence had been approved and read to the men who made up the Continental Army.
That Declaration represen ted the collective work of all the 56 men who
were to sign it, including some nine or mo re Master Masons, but it reflected specifically the words of Thomas Jefferson who authored the immortal documen t, with the sage and wise counsel of our Brother Benjamin
Franklin seated at his right hand to assist in the formation of the dramatic
and momentous phrases.
It was time for the document to be signed. and our Brother John Hancock approaches the table, takes the quill pen in hand and affixes his
signature in oversize and bold character s, remarkin g that he wanted
George III to be abk to read his name without the need of spectacles.
My Brethren . if such a document lay on the table before you today,
would vour signature be there?
It is 'now the winter of 1777 and o ur Brother, George Washingto n, is
encamped with his me n at Valley Forge. Pennsylvania . The weathe.r is
freezing cold . Many of the men are without shoes or adequate clothing.
They huddle in small groups around the ca mpfi res before their log huts.
This is the Continen tal Army, comman ded by that renowned Brother,
General George Washington , and it is this group which holds in its hands,
the destiny of the United Colonies in their struggle to gain independence.
Many of these voluntee rs are Master Masons, as we learn from the
records of the Army or Military Lodges of the day, which have endured
the ravages of tim e. It will not be until June of 1778. however, that the
troops will have completed their training under our Brothe r. Baron Fred.
erick von Steuben, and will leave Valley Forge.

Wilcox:
"There are two kinds of people on earth today,
Just two kinds of people, no more. I say.
Not the good and the bad, for 'tis well understood
The good are half bad and the bad are half good.
Not the happy and sad, for the swift flying y~ars
Bring each man his laughter and each man his_ tears.
Not the rich and the poor. for to count a mans wealth
You must first know the state of his conscience and health.
Not the humble and proud, for in life's busy span
Who puts on vain airs is not counted a man.
No! The two kinds of people on earth I mean
Are the people who lift, and the people who lean.
Wherever you go you will find the world's masses
Are ever divided in just these two classes,
And strangely enough. you find . too, I wean ,
There is only one lifter to twenty who Jean .
This o ne question I ask. Are you easing the load
Of overtaxed lifte rs who toil down the road?
Or are yo u a leaner who lets othe rs bear "
Your portion of worry and labor and care ?

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO THE ORDINANCES

to Provide For Use of Lowest Number (See 1982 Proceedings, page 35).

1982 GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION NO. 3
CONSOLIDATION TERMS TO PROVIDE FOR USE OF
LOWEST NUMBER
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Recommendation No. 3 of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master recommends that when two or more Constituent
Lodges consolidate, the consolidated Lodge shall at all events bear the
number of the oldest consolidating Lodge.
To carry out the Grand Master's intent, your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED, that Section 2104 of the California Masonic Code be
amended by deleting the 3rd paragraph thereof, and adding in lieu thereof
the following: "The Lodge thus formed shall bear the lowest number of
any Lodge thus consolidating, and may bear the name of any one or more
of the Lodges consolidating. The consolidated Lodge, if it bears the name
and number of the lowest numbered Lodge, may retain the Charter and
Seal of that Lodge, but if it bears the number of that Lodge and another
name, may receive, without charge, a new charter and provide a new seal,

201

or may have the authorization of such consolidation by the Grand Lodge
endorsed on the charter of the lowest numbered Lodge."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

At the 1982 Annual Communication Grand Master West recommended
that consolidating Lodges be free to select a name of their choice but must
elect to retain the lowest number of the Lodges consolidating.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is sympathetic to then
Grand Master West's desire to retain the histQries of consolidating Lodges.
Research into the manner in which Lodge history is retained reveals
that while history never is "lost," in the pure sense of the word, it can be
relegated to a "back shelf" so that it is not easily attainable. Your Commit.tee is cognizant of the desire to retain the geneology of every Lodge
which has been chartered by this Grand Lodge whether or not it is currently active on the rolls of Grand Lodge.
Also, the California Masonic Code is not specific as to the manner in
which a Lodge resulting from the consolidation of two or more Lodges is
to be issued a charter.
Further, while the Code specifies that consolidating Lodges may take
the name and/or number of either of the Lodges, actual practice reveals
that in some instances, an entirely new name has been selected.
This Commi.ttee believes that there is a possibility that a Lodge deserving of and needing consolidation might be denied that negotiable prerogative should rules require that they must choose the lower number of
those Lodges negotiating a consolidation.
For example, an old Lodge with a low number but with a small membership and poor finances, might desire to consolidate with a young Lodge,
with a high number and extensive resources. Should Masonic Law dictate
that the members negotiating a consolidation be required to select the
lower number of the Lodges, it is possible that the younger Lodge, preferring to retain their own number, would deny consolidation. With no
other Lodge with which to attempt consolidation, the older Lodge might
have to surrender its charter and go out of existance.
These problem areas can be resolved, but your Committee does not
believe that adoption of the carryover Recommendation would accomplish
the desired purpose.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that the
incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to study the subject of Lodge
consolidations together with the preservation of their histories.
Therefore, we recommend a "No" vote on this carryover recommendation.
Not Ad9pted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REVISE FIRST DEGREE LECTURE QUALIFICATION OF JUNIOR WARDEN
(1982 Resolution No. 1)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Carryover Resolution No. 2, (1982 Resolution No. 1) proposes to revise
the First Degree Lecture by not requiring the Junior Warden to memorize
the portion of the lecture printed in the Monitor and Officers' Manual.
The Resolution also makes optional the delivery of that portion of the
lecture to Candidates.
Last year your Committee on Policy and General Purposes opposed the
Resolution for reasons which were then stated. Some members of the
Committee still oppose the Resolution for those reasons. However, the
Committee has now changed its position and recommends a "Yes" vote.
There is a basic policy question involved in every attempt to make
changes in ritual. This is particularly true when there are recommendations
for shortening the ritual or making it "easier."
We learn our Masonic lessons from ritual. Any shortening of those lessons deprives a Candidate of the very material that presumably aids in
making him a better man.
We form our impressions of the seriousness of Masonry from what we
hear, though perhaps not always as we receive the degree. Many times we
learn the lesson as we listen to later repetitions.
These points argue against the Resolution.
On the other hand the point is made that it is increasingly difficult to
obtain officers in many Lodges. Those things which lessen the duties of
an officer may make it easier to obtain officers.
It is also argued that the Candidate is in a daze, that little of what he
th~n hears is unde~stood or retained; thus it does not really cause him to
have or fail to have an impression of Masonry.
The disputes with regard to ritual will persist. And, unless past trends
change, the Grand Lodge will properly be conservative in its approach to
that change.
But this proposal is different from most. From 1924 to 1957 our ritual
was as this Resolution would have it be. There is no discernible difference
in the quality of Masons made when this monitorial portion. of our ritual
was not learned or given as compared to those made when it was given.
This Grand Lodge respects and jealously guards our ritual from exci·
sions or modifications.
However, your Committee believes this modification to be appropri'"'I!
at this time. We would not want it regarded as a precedent for expected
approval of future proposed changes in the ritual.
Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

203

The Committee on Ritual:

.Brethren, the. ~r.and Lecturer and the Ritual Committee are charged
with the responsibility of preserving the ritual as it has been handed down
from time immemorial. The intent of this resolution is self-explanatory
and has been supported by the majority vote of this Grand Lodge. In the
past, changes have been made in the Monitor without the consent of the
Grand Lodge. Beca.use this R~so~u.tion is for the good of the Fraternity,
as a ~h?le, and not JUSt for an individual Lodge, it should not be necessary
at this time to enumerate the many benefits of this Resolution. Your continued .support is needed to restore this portion of the Monitor to what it
was pnor to 1957. The restoration of the First Degree Lecture to its pre1957 form and to ~om~ly with .our responsibility, is more important now
than at any other time m the history of this great Jurisdiction. This is for
the good. of our Frat~rnity. Brethren, we need your help!!
The Ritual Committee unanimously recommends a "Yes" vote.
Adopted.

PER CAPITA TAX -

VOTE BY SECRET BALLOT
(1)

1:he propone~t of this legislation has concern that the vote on the per
capita tax, special assessments, and other assessments collected with the
pe~ capita tax upon the members may not be accurately determined by a
voice, hand, or rising ballot.
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, several of the votes taken on the increase of the per capita
tax and other special assessments of the Grand Lodge have been extremely
close to call by use of a hand or standing ballot:
RESOLVED that Section 250 of the California Masonic Code be
amended to read as· follows:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Section 250. MANNER OF VOTING. All questions in the Grand
Lodge, except election of officers, and matters pertaining to the per
capita tax, special assessments, and other assessments collected with the
per capita tax, shall be decided either by voice, hand, a rising vote or
by written ballot, as the Grand Master shall direct, unless, before the
announcement of the result thereof, three members eligible to vote shall
demand that the vote be taken by written ballot, in which case it shall
be thus taken. Voting on matters pertaining to the per capita tax, special
assessments, and other assessments collected with the per capita tax,
shall be by written ballot only."

. To avoid any confusion in the direction of this report let it be known,
m advance, that the Committee on Policy and General Purposes opposes
this Resolution.
Based on our experience in attending the Communications of this Grand
Lodge we believe that Grand Masters in the past have exercised keen
judgment in determining the outcome of all matters that have been put
before t~e delegate~. In fact, Grand Masters have, on their own, called
~or a wntten ballot if there was the slightest doubt in the balance of the
issue at hand. We are confident that Grand Masters in the future will be
equally.obedient to the rules of good judgment and fair play.

C.M.C.; it reads as follows:

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Finance.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 1 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponent of this Resolution has concern that the vote on the per
capita tax, special assessments, and other assessments collected with the
per capita tax upon the members may not be accurately determined by a
voice, hand, or rising vote.
To carry out the intent of the proponent, your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED that Section 250 of the California Masonic Code be
amended to read as follows:
"Section 250. MANNER OF VOTING. All questions in the Grand
Lodge, except election of Officers, and matters pertaining to the per
capita tax, special assessments, and other assessments collected with the
per capita tax, shall be decided either by voice, hand, a rising vote or
by written ballot, as the Grand Master shall direct, unless, before the
announcement of the result thereof, three members eligible to vote shall
demand that the vote be taken by written ballot, in which case it shall
be thus taken. Voting on matters pertaining to the election of Officers,
per capita tax, special assessments, and other assessments collected with
the per capita tax, shall be by written ballot only."
To place the matter before the Grand lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponent of Resolution Number 1 seeks to require a mandatory
written ballot on all matters pertaining to the Per Capita Tax.

205

"All q~estio~s in the Grand Lodge, except the election of Officers, shall
be decided either by voice, hand, a rising vote or by written ballot, as
the Grand Master shall direct, unless, before the announcement of the
results thereof, three members shall demand that the vote be taken by
written ballot, in which case it shall thus be taken."
It is the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
!hat there are sufficient votin~ safeguards in the present law to protect the
mterests of all members. A time-consuming mandatory written ballot, to
include matters that might otherwise be uncontested, is an unnecessary
burden to place on the delegates of this Grand Lodge.
We, therefore, recommend a "No" vote.

The Committee on Finance:

The Committee· on Finance concurred in the recommendation of the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Not Adopted.

2. Number contributing.
3. Proportion of members contributing.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

207

4. Total of contributions received.
5. Average contribution per member.
6. Amount needed to be on the 'Honor Roll'."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution would add a new subsection to Section No. 2548 of the
California Masonic Code, which lists the required duties of a Lodge Secretary, and proposes to make it mandatory for the Secretary to write to
the members of his Lodge in April, May, June and July, and inform them
as to the status of the Lodge's participation in contributions to the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund; and the proposed subsection also sets forth the
minimum information the Secretary shall be required to place in the written communication to the Lodge members.
While it is obvious that the proponents of this resolution hope that
repeated mailing of updated information and requests for funds will produce more and greater gifts to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund,
your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that the proposed repeated mailing of the required information could prove redundant
and not beneficial. As a majority of our Lodges do not have trestleboards,
these required mailings would be an increased cost to those Lodges without
trestleboards. In addition, in cases where the Lodge quota has been
reached, subsequent mailing of this information could result in no further
contributions.
The Committee whole-heartedly supports all efforts to increase contributions to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund but believes that this
resolution is unnecessary and places increased costs on many Lodges, as
well as undue requirements upon the Lodge Secretary. Therefore, the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
Masonic Homes Endowment Board:
No report presented.
Not Adopted.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
. This resolution purports to delete the words "registered letter" and "certified mail" from Section 2814 of the California Masonic Code and to
substitute therefor the words "restricted delivery mail."
It also changes the word actual to the word personal in dealing with
service by the tiler.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

210

Postal regulations (Reg. 933-1) require that to obtain the new restricted
delivery, the letter be sent either registered or by certified mail. Thus there
really is no deletion but only the addition of restricted delivery. Restricted
delivery is delivery to the addressee only or to his duly authorized agent.
This is the only new requirement imposed.
We oppose this for two reasons:
1) Expense. The added expense is $1.00 per letter.
2) Difficulty and delay in obtaining service.
The change of the word personal for the word actual appears intended
to accomplish the same result.
The proponent has told us of unfortunate incidents within his experience
where properly mailed letters were signed for by others than the addressee
and never received by him .
We agree that these are unfortunate experiences but have also been
informed that in addition to the expense, there will be delay because a
Brother is unavailable, then must travel to the post office, etc.
The benefit appears to your Committee to be outweighed by the cost
and delay.
We recommend a "No" vote.

PLAYING OF BINGO GAMES BY TENANTS

(9)

The proponent of this Resolution seeks to permit tenants in buildings
owned by Masonic organizations to play bingo where permitted by law as
to non-profit, charitable organizations.
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the CMC appears to be unclear to solve the question of
the acceptability of bingo playing by tenants on Temple property; and,
WHEREAS, charitable and non- profit organizations are permitted to
play bingo by statute or ordinance in many communities within our Jurisdiction; and,
WHEREAS, many Lodges are faced with continually escalating operating costs and could directly benefit from the increased tenant usage of
their facilities:
RESOLVED that Section 3314 of the California Masonic Code be
amended by adding at the end the following:
"Bingo playing by non-profit, charitable tenants of a Masonic owned
building, where permitted by law is specifically exempted from the provisions of this Section."

RESOLVED FURTHER that Annotation 2026b of the California Masonic Code be deleted.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Resolution No. 9 proposes to amend Section 3314 C.M.C., to permit
bingo playing by non-profit, charitable tenants of a Masonic owned building where permitted by local ordinance.
The California State Legislature adopted Section 326.5 of the California
Penal Code, which limits playing bingo to those cities and counties which
have adopted an ordinance allowing bingo to be played only by and for
the benefit of charities to which a gift would be tax exempt.
Section 326.5 of the Penal Code requires that any bingo game must be
conducted by a non-profit, charitable organization on property owned or
leased by it and used as its office or to conduct its activities. Lodges are
not non-profit, charitable organizations and, accordingly, cannot legally
conduct bingo games.
Section 326.5 of the Penal Code states that all bingo games must be
open to the public. Our Masonic law does not allow the use of Masonic
premis~s to conduct public or private gambling enterprises.
. Section 3314 C.M.C. specifically provides that no Lodge or Mason shall
directly or indirectly give or attempt to give aid or countenance of Masonry

Grand Master Maynard commented on the new cloth insignias adorning
the podiums and the altar. He further commented on the $4,000.00 gift
presented to the Masonic Homes by the Northern California DeMolay
Association. This contribution is to be used for the development of "Point
DeMolay" which will be an overlook of the Rainbow Park now in the
process of development at the Covina Home.

Several jurisdictions instituted or recommended Masonic booths at state
and county fairs. Wisconsin's program included a continuous slide show
and audio accompaniment telling the story of Freemasonry, and distribution of inform~tional material. Minnesota carried out a similar program
at the state fatr - a continuous slide show entitled "Famous Masons"
which depicted famous Masons, past and present, in all walks of life.
Minnesota also developed a ''Minnesota Mason" decal, which was mailed
to all members with a Jetter from the Grand Master "proudly proclaiming
Maso!lry'~ importance in Minn_esota," and a reply envelope requesting a
contnbution to defray cost. Minnesota also set a budget for their Public
Information Committee, including funding for a full-time Public Information Director.
Not all Masonic bodies responded to membership losses so positively.
Grand Master Ferguson of West Virginia noted with concern that "some
of our appendent organizations, fearful of their own future, have seized
upon our loss of membership as an excuse to interfere with the internal
affairs of_ this Grand Lodge. Examples: the portrayal of the play, "Traitor,"
the showing of the film "Symbol of Pride;" both have been declared illegal.
We shall never and shall not now condone nor practice recruitment ethical
or otherwise.
'
EDUCATION: Almost all jurisdictions have shown a strong interest in
Masonic education. This has taken the form not only of programs for the
officers of the Lodges such as District Meetings, Schools of Instruction
Leadership Workshops, and similar activities, but also instruction for th~
average Brother. The feeling is widely expressed that the Masonic education of a Brother too often ceases after his attaining the Third Degree,
and ~his hiatus is a c9ntributing factor in the loss of interest evidenced by
demits and suspensions for non-payment of dues. An example of programs
designed for ".Seyond the Ritual" education of the average Mason is Nevada's education program on researched Masonic subjects, made available
to all Lodges. Perhaps it is coincidence, but we note that in 1981 Nevada's
membership loss was 29 (.4% ), and in 1982 they showed a gain of 3 members.
FINANCES: Most Grand Jurisdictions appear to be in excellent finan~ial condition in co~trast to membership Joss, and show substantial receipts
in excess of expenditures. Massachusetts showed a $993,135 increase in its
general fund in 1980, and Pennsylvania an increase of $1,004,798 in 1981.
CHARITY: Almost all Grand Jurisdictions have charitable activities
including Homes for the elderly and/or destitute, orphanages, stipends fo;
the destitute, and in one case (Victoria, Australia) a Freemason's hospital.
North Carolina has a combined Masonic/Order of Eastern Star Home
which has seen 956 residents come and go in 69 years. Virginia has 73
residents in its Home, with a cost of $1,000,000 annually, with an income
of $1,300,000. Maine awarded $106,000 in 1981 to 44 applicants for financial assistance.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
REVIEW OF PROCEEDINGS
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In 1982-1983 your Committee reviewed some 40 publications from
Grand Jurisdictions in amity with the Grand Lodge of California. Of these,
26 were from Grand Lodges in the United States of America, and 14 from
foreign jurisdictions.
In our annual report, we do not attempt to detail the activities of these
bodies, but rather to present information as to the position of Freemasonry
on both a nationwide and worldwide basis. We do not attempt to give
detailed data on membership, finances, committee actions and similar matters except as they may be of an unusual nature. We do attempt to indicate
trends within the Fraternity.
MEMBERSHIP: Out of 32 Grand Jurisdictions which supplied membership data, 30 showed membership losses ranging from 5% (Japan and
Victoria-Australia) to .4% (South Carolina). Two showed membership
gains - Nevada, which gained 3 members in 1982, and North Carolina,
which showed a .1% gain in 1982. Average membership loss in reporting
jurisdictions is 2.3%. Loss of members is largely due to (1) death and (2)
suspension for non-payment of dues. Victoria (Australia) and Alberta
(Canada) both showed 37% due to death. Pennsylvania showed 66% and
Minnesota 59%. In the United States most jurisdictions showed 50% or
more of their losses due to death. Membership world-wide seems to have
peaked around 1960, with a steady decline ever since.
The continuing membership Joss has evoked concern from almost all
Grand Jurisdictions whose reports we have reviewed. We note the effort
of our own Grand Lodge in the newspaper supplement published last year.
We note in the 1982 Proceedings of the Conference of Grand Masters of
North America that the film "Symbols of Pride" is described as a "means
of ethical recruitment." Victoria urges "precept and example to the community by Masons and Masonic bodies." Pennsylvania recommends exposing Freemasonry to the community; participating in Masonic attire at
appropriate occasions; media notices of time and place of Masonic meetings; and signs at community entrances. The Grand Master of Pennsylvania
appointed a Public Information Committee to prepare public information
programs, including T. V. documentaries, pamphlets for public distribution,
and radio messages.

separate scholarships); Minnesota in 1982 awarded four $1,000, four $750,
and four $500 schol;uships; Virginia awarded 66 scholarships for $18,050;
and New Brunswick (Canada) awarded seven $1,000 scholarships. West
Virginia has $1,200,000 in its scholarship fund.
LIFE MEMBERSHIPS: Two Grand Jurisdictions reported functional
Life Membership programs - Nevada, with 365 participants, and Montana.
MISCELLANY: The Freemasons Hospital of Victoris (Australia) in the
last 6 months of 1981 had 3,597 in-patients. 15% were Masonic.
In his Annual Address in 1982, the Grand Master of West Virginia
strongly condemned "frivolity" in the 2nd section of the Third Degree,
and also stated that "I do not believe any Mason has the right, or has
earned that right, to tell a risque or off-colored joke or story in a Masonic
Lodge." Georgia reported that for the first time in its history a Lodge
(Solomon's No. 1) received an official visitation from the officers of another Grand Lodge; in this case, Pennsylvania. The visitation was on February 13, 1982, and Grand Master Whitlock, and other Grand Officers of
Georgia were in attendance. In a less festive vein, it was discovered that
$350,000 of Grand Lodge funds had been embezzled by a Past Grand
Master/Grand Treasurer. The DeKalb County Grand Jury returned an
indictment against the erring "Brother."
In Pennsylvania, resolutions are submitted semi-annually to Grand
Lodge, but are voted upon annually.
In Tennessee, degrees must be at least 28 days apart.
Main presented 3,000 "Broken Column" pins to Masonic widows in
1981. In Maine, each Lodge is required to present an annual "history" to
Grand Lodge, or pay a $10 fine. One Lodge is presently 23 years in arrears!
Where else but in "Yankee" Maine!
In Denmark the Grand Lodge won a seven year court battle with the
Danish State Broadcasting Company, which had planned to broadcast a
T. V. program with the intent of putting the Fraternity to ridicule. The
court decision ordered the original film and all copies to be destroyed.
Another happy event was a visit of 180 Masons and their wives from the
Grand Lodge of Illinois to the Grand Lodge of Denmark.
The Grand Lodge of South Australia elects its Grand Master for a 3
year term. They have a Homes Endowment Fund in excess of $7 ,000,000.
The "Texas Freemason" has a "Looking Backward" section which recalls
past Masonic events.
The Grand Lodge of Washington, D.C., has reduced its ritual to writing.
The single copy is in the repository of the Grand Secretary's safe.
In Wyoming, 18 year olds may petition for the Masonic degrees.
Virginia passed a resolution permitting the Master of a Lodge to appoint
Chaplain, Stewards, Marshall, Organist and Tiler from Brethren not members of his Lodge. A resolution requiring a one year wait or completion
of the Third Degree proficiency before making application for membership
in an appendent body was rejected by the Grand Lodge.
We note that among distinguished Masons, Senator Jesse Helms was
Grand Orator for the Grand Lodge of North Carolina in 1981.

Lastly, in Oklahoma, Grand Master Haney on November 3, 1981 upheld
the Masonic sovereignty of the Grand Master of a Grand Jurisdiction by
prohibiting any activity in connection with Scottish Masonry by a Mason
in Oklahoma. This action was rescinded on December 2, 1981 after a
problem with AASR was solved to Grand Master Haney's satisfaction.

Notable books purchased were a 7-volume history of California by H.
H. Bancroft, "60th Anniversary of No. California DeMolay,'' History of
the "Acacia Fraternity,'' "Stephen A. Douglas - Freemason,'' "Trial of
the Templars,'' "Faith and Fraternalism,'' a history of the Knights of Co-lumbus, "Hooded Americanism,'' a history of the Ku Klux Klan; "A Documentary History of Prince Hall and Other Black Fraternal Orders." We
also acquired an audio "Masonic Leadership" course from the Masonic
Service Association in Silver Springs, Maryland, consisting of 5 cassette
tapes on which are recorded 10 lessons with a 90 page workbook with
questions and answers and a guide for action, cartoons and practical suggestions for "growing Leaders." Additionally, we acquired a tape of California Lodge music and also a tape of 4 old Masonic songs recorded in
the early phonograph records. In addition to the above, we now have 20
cassette tapes from the Oregon Research Lodge on which are recorded
talks and discussions on a variety of subjects.
Notable among the donated books is a 40 volume Library of American
History, Masonic histories and comparative religion donated by Herb
Headen.
Our Museum collection was enriched by donations of a number of Masonic aprons, buttons, pins, glass tumblers and ceramic plates. We also
received several items of Masonic Philately, a German envelope with
Square and Compass printed on the cover, and an envelope from the Island
of Barbados of 1976 with a stamp showing the presumed likeness of Prince
Hall and the Square and Compass.
During the year the following research studies were undertaken by the
members of the Library staff:
1. Origin and source of Masonic watch fob opening to form a cross.
2. Mrs. Jewett regarding history and photos of old Grand Lodge Temple
on Van Ness Ave. and Market St., San Francisco.
3. S. Solomon - the esoterica accounts of King Solomon's Temple.
4. Search of entire holdings for material on Jamestown Lodge No. 54
Temple Building for historical society.
5. Search files for material on pottery ware from the old Temple destroyed by fire on Post and Market Streets.
During the past year we had the good fortune to have a lost book
returned - "The Greek Origin of Freemasonry", lost in 1980 and recently
found and returned. Three books were lost to a Brother who died and his
heirs could not find the whereabouts of "DeMolay Handbook," "Freemasonry and Roman Catholicism" and "The Trial of the Templars." Unfortunately the second item is out of print, and the price of the other two
has risen to almost double.
We are still assisting Mr. Tony Fells in his study of our Fraternity; his
studies at Stanford are scheduled to be completed by this December when
his book, "The Masonic Fraternity in San Francisco During the Guilded
Age 1870-1900" will have been completed.
During the past year, shelves were purchased and placed along two walls
in the second room on the south side of the second floor, helping immeasurably in sorting out items going to and from the larger storage area.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTE E ON TAXATION
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Grand Lodge Committee on Taxation renders advice on matters of
taxation when requested by the Grand Lodge, subordinate Lodges and
other organizations under their jurisdiction. Our assistance has been requested with respect to matters of income, property, sales and employment
taxes. Our work includes this annual report which discusses items of current interest in the taxation of fraternal organizations.
In our 1982 Report, we advised that Lodges and Temple Associations
would be excused from filing Federal Form 990 with respect to tax years

GRAND WDGE OF CALIFORNIA

225

ending after 1982 if gross receipts are not in excess of $25,000. California
has now adopted a similar change which permits Lodges and Temple Associations with annual gross receipts of $25,000 or less to file the simplified
information return, Form 199B.
Our 1982 Report also commented upon the "California Split Roll Property Tax Initiative" and its possibly harmful effect if passed on fraternal
organizations owning real property in California. That initiative failed to
qualify for the ballot as the required number of signatures was not collected within the statutory period.
Recently, the Committee was asked whether contributions given to local
Lodges are deductible for income tax purposes. Contributions by an individual to a domestic fraternal order operating under the Lodge system,
such as Masonic Lodges, are deductible for income tax purposes only if
the contributions will be used exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, literary, or educational purposes, or for the prevention of cruelty to
children or animals. Internal Revenue Code Section 170(c)(4). For example, a charitable purpose is the support of elderly and indigent members
of the order who live in a home owned by the order. I.T. 3261, CB 19391, 122. Thus, contributions to the Homes Endowment Fund for the support
of the Ho"?-e at Union City are deductible even though given to the Lodge
for transmittal to the Homes Endowment Fund rather than sent directly
to the Fund. However, contributions given to a Lodge for the use of a
local Blood Bank are not deductible unless the Blood Bank:s operations
qualify it as a charitable organization. Typically, this would require the
Blood Bank to limit its aid to poor and distressed members of the Fraternity and their families. Because most Blood Banks do not so operate, it
is unlikely that contributions to the Lodge for the use of a local Blood
Bank would be deductible.
Historically, -individuals could deduct charitable contributions for income tax purposes only if they itemized their deductions. Recently, the
Congress and California State Legislature enacted provisions which allow
individuals to deduct charitable contributions even though itemized deductions are not claimed. On 1982 and 1983 Federal Income Tax returns,
an individual who does not itemize deductions may deduct 25% of his first
$100 of charitable contributions. In 1984, he may deduct 25% of his first
$300 of charitable contributions. In 1985, he may deduct 50% of all charitable contributions and in 1986 may deduct all charitable contributions,
subject to a limitation of 50% of adjusted gross income. California has
adopted similar rules for 1984, 1985 and 1986 only. In California, the
overall limitation is 20% of adjusted gross income rather than the 50% of
adjusted gross income limit for federal purposes. Both the federal and the
California deductions are due to expire at the end of 1986. It should be
noted that the charitable contribution deduction for taxpayers who do
itemize their deductions has not been changed and is scheduled to continue
beyond 1986. These changes were enacted to encourage charitable contributions by those persons who do not normally itemize their deductions.
Lodges may wish to use this information to encourage contributions for
the charitable works of our Grand Lodge.

With respect to the reimbursement of Grand Lodge Officers, Staff,
Committeemen, Inspectors, etc., for use of their personal cars on Grand
Lodge business, we again confirm our established policy which does not
include such fixed costs as depreciation, insurance, etc., in said reimbursement rate.
While the Committee recognizes that fuel prices have generally stabilized and that many new vehicles are capable of producing more miles to
the gallon than in years past, our recommendation is that our present rate
of reimbursement is appropriate for the ensuing year.
The rate of reimbursement for the use of personal vehicles on Grand
Lodge business shall therefore remain at $ .18 per mile until this time
again in 1984.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the audited financial statements presented by the Grand Treasurer for the fiscal year ended June 30,
1983 as required by our Code. Costs to operate your Grand Lodge for the
past year decreased over the previous period ended June 30, 1982, and
were more than 11 % under the Grand Lodge budget. The Grand Master
is to be commended for his efforts in controlling costs throughout the year.
Nearly all committees operated within their budgeted appropriations and
we congratulate all for observing such excellent fiscal responsibility.
Approval by the Grand Master for supplementary appropriations in the
amount of $70,400 has been given to cover those items where budgets
were exceeded.
Estimates on the publication and distribution costs for our official magazine, The California Freemason, indicate that our present per capita assessment of $1.00 will be adequate for the coming year and no increase
will be required.

229

New Telephone System ...................... .. ............. $20,000
Three (3) Typewriters . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 3,600
One (1) Data Terminal . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 3,000
Total. ......... . ............................................ $26,600
It seems appropriate that this Committee should comment on the disturbing trend of our declining membership, especially since those numbers
play a direct role in the cost of operations of the Grand Lodge. During
the period between 1972 and the present, our assessable membership has
declined from 226,712 to 181,794 members as of June 30, 1983, a loss of
almost 45,000 members or nearly 20%.
Because our per capita assessment is directly related to the number of
assessable members, this constant decline causes a continually escalating
share of Grand Lodge cost to be borne by the individual Lodges, even
given the unlikely situation that our operating costs do not escalate.
Your elected Grand Lodge Officers are all very aware of this problem
and have, each one in turn, endeavored to fashion programs for the Craft
which are designed to reverse this frightening trend. While we are confident that our Masonic leadership with the support of all earnest and dedicated Masons will ultimately enhance the role Masonic activity enjoys in
this Jurisdiction and bring about a positive trend in our membership numbers, it will not occur overnight. During that interim period, this Committee will work closely with our Masonic leaders to control both the costs
of operations, and programs and to ht:lp bring about judicious "belt tightening" wherever and whenever possible.
This Committee once again offers its thanks to Very Worshipful John
A. Sickenberger, Grand Treasurer, for his invaluable assistance and guidance. His knowledge and wisdom in financial affairs continues to be one
of the great assets of this Grand Lodge. To Hugo Delfin, our Accounting
Manager, new Master Mason, and his staff, our heartfelt thanks for a
superior job.
Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, and his staff are due our special
appreciation for their cheerful assistance at all times.

ANNUAL ELECTION OF OFFICERS
Grand Master Maynard announced that the hour had arrived for the
Annual Election of the Grand Lodge Officers. The Grand Secretary then
read the Section of the Constitution of Grand Lodge which pertained to
the election of Officers. The results of the elections were as follow:
The R:.W:.E. Arthur Haglund, Acalanes-Fellowship Lodge No. 480,
was elected Grand Master.

INSTALLATION OF OFFICERS
The Installation Ceremony commenced at 2:00 P.M., with the retiring
Grand Master, Most Worshipful Harry L. Maynard, acting as Installing
Officer, and Past Grand Master Donald B. McCaw acting as Master of
Ceremonies. In accordance with Ritual, all of the Appointive Officers were
duly installed after which the Grand Lecturer, Grand Secretary and Grand
Treasurer were installed. The Junior Grand Warden and Senior Grand
Warden were then installed in their respective stations. The Deputy Grand
Master was then installed after which the Grand Master was duly installed.
Grand Master E. Arthur Haglund expressed his appreciation to the
Installing Officer and the Master of Ceremonies, and he invited each of
the Elective Officers to introduce those members of their families who
were in attendance. Employees of the Grand Lodge Office Staff were
asked to rise for recognition. The Appointed Grand Lodge Officers were
asked to introduce their wives for recognition. The retiring Grand Lodge
Officers and their ladies were then presented to the audience. The newly
installed Grand Master then requested the Grand Marshal to present the

236

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

wife of the Junior Past Grand Master, Carolyn Maynard, to the East, and
called upon the Grand Secretary who graciously presented her with a gift
on behalf of _the entire me~bership of the Fraternity. This charming lady
responded with an expression of love and affection in appreciation of the
remembrance. Lady Carolyn was then presented with a beautiful bouquet
of roses for which she expressed her thanks.
Past Grand Master Robert 0. West presented to the Junior Past Grand
Master, the Past Grand Master's apron. Past Grand Master Vernon L.
Gordon then presented the Grand Master's lapel pin to the retiring Grand
Master, following which he was presented with the Past Grand Master's
Certificate by Past Grand Master Kermit A. Jacobson. The Past Grand
Master's :8adge was p~esented b~ Past Gran~ Master Raymond A. Ebbage.
Appropnate words with expressions of gratitude accompanied each of the
above presentations.
Soloist Doris Hatlen, accompanied by Grand Organist James C. Myers,
t~en serenaded the newly installed Grand Master and his lovely lady Barbie. Members of the Haglund family were introduced by the Grand Master.
Members of Acalanes Fellowship Lodge No. 480 were then recognized.
Potentate Robert L. Nicolai of Aahmes Shrine Temple presented the
newly installed Grand Master with a "Grand Master's" Jeweled Fez and a
special belt buckle commemorating the East-West Shrine Football Classic.
The retiring Grand Master met with the new Grand Master, the Deputy
Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand Wardens at the altar where the
respective lapel pins of their offices were exchanged.
The Grand Master's son and daughter, Cathy and Jim, presented their
father with a cassette recorder, and Grand Master William Brass of Montana presented a plaque to the Grand Master informing him of his membership in the Royal Order of Big Fork Lodge No. 150.
Grand Master Haglund then addressed the assembled guests. He expressed his appreciation to all in attendance for taking the time to be with
him on this occasion. He spoke of his program for the year and the goals
that he hoped to achieve. The importance of each individual Brother and
his participation in the Grand Lodge programs during the coming year was
stressed. He stated that with all of our Brethren working together we hope
to change the present decline in membership to a positive upward trend.
This can be accomplished by every member contributing his best effort.
The slogan this year is, "One Mason Can Make A Difference - You!"
At the conclusion of the Grand Master's installation message he was
accorded a standing ovation.
Following the Benediction, the assembled guests retired for a reception
to greet the newly installed Grand Lodge Officers.
All business of the 134th Annual Communication was completed at 5:10
P.M. after which the newly installed Grand Master announced that Grand
Lodge would be called on at 9:00 A.M. on Thursday, October 13, 1983
for the purpose of closing.

proceeds from sale or retirement are included in income.

ORGANIZATION:
The Masonic Homes Pooled Income fund vas organized on October 15,
1974 aru is a charitable remainder trust t.o which donors contribute
irrevocable remainder interests in property vhile retaining an income
interest for life for one or more beneficiaries. The donors are
entitled to a tax deduction equivalent to the present value of the
remainder interest in the property contributed.
The property transferred by such donor is held in trust ~y the
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Furn aM. lB comingled vith and invested and reinvested vith other properties transferred to the fund. All income of the Furn is distributed quarterly
to the beneficiaries, based on their proportionate share of the
Pool. Upon the death of each donor ' s l ast income benefi~iary •. the
remainder interest is distributed t.o Masonic Homes of California, a
charitable corporation.

NOTE 2 - SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
Method of Accounting:
The financial statements are prepared on the accrual basis of
accounting.
Investments:
Investments are reported at their fair market value as of June

30. Propertiee contributed during the year by donors are recorded at
their fair market value at date of receipt and investments pirch.ased
are recorded at cost. The adjustment to the furrl balance required at
year end to report investments at their then fair market value is
recorded as net change in market value of investments.

NOTE 3 - FEDIBAL AND STATE INCOME TAXES:
The Furn pa.ya no income tax on income distributed to beneficiaries. Applicable federal and state income taxes are JBid by the
beneficia:riee on their share of distributed income.
